meta.blurb: Dara leaves the office with her things in a box and feels she has nothing left. Her neighbour Hugo, a retired firefighter, asks her to do one small hard thing every day. A charity ten-kilometre run is twelve weeks away.
meta.bible: Dara: a woman of twenty-nine who loses her job at a shoe company and rebuilds her confidence over about one year, and the main character. Hugo: her neighbour, a retired Firefighter in his sixties, who walks with her and helps her practise. Leila: Dara's older sister. Setting: a city, a small flat, a park and a river path. The race: a charity ten-kilometre run, twelve weeks after she signs up. Key terms: Comfort zone, Firefighter, Counsellor, Kerb, Resilient, Interview. Voice: kind, honest and practical; each beat shows one idea about resilience. The science is real and hedged: slow breathing can calm the body, naming feelings can reduce their force, most people recover well from hard events, and serious distress needs a doctor or counsellor. Marlow Shoes: the shoe company where Dara worked for six years, in customer orders; it closes. Alder Road: where Dara and Hugo live, in neighbouring houses; Dara has a first-floor flat, Hugo the house next door with a gate. Pepper: Hugo's old spaniel who walks slowly. Hugo is sixty-eight and was at Station Six for thirty years. Linden Park: the park with the long hill and the bench; the river path runs beside it. Mina: Dara's friend from Marlow Shoes. Tomas: another friend. Ines: a woman in her sixties, a slow runner, whom Dara meets on the river path. Jo: the friendly assistant at Stride Sports, the running shop. Riverside Ten: the charity ten-kilometre run for a local food bank, starting at the Town Hall and finishing in Linden Park. Brightwell Supplies: where Dara takes a three-month temporary office job; her manager is Ms Barrow and her colleague is Kofi. Dr Anand: Dara's doctor. Ben: a nineteen-year-old new neighbour in flat three. Ms Hale: a counsellor. Leila is thirty-four, a teacher, with two children, Samir, six, and Nadia, four. Timeline: she loses her job in March, signs up for the Riverside Ten about two months later, runs it twelve weeks after that, and the book ends the following March. Halden Logistics: the firm that interviews Dara and chooses someone else. Gareth: a friend who complains too much. Town Hall: where the Riverside Ten starts. Her race number is 1127; Ines runs the race too. Dara's old maths exam at sixteen, failed, is found in Leila's attic. Hugo has a scar on his knee from running on an injury and later needs a knee operation. The community pool is in Linden Park. Dara's habits: three good things each night, worry time at six, a list of hard things on the fridge, a Sunday review. This book is general information and is not a substitute for medical or mental health care; if you feel unsafe, speak to a doctor or a local crisis service.
chapters: Rest Is Part of the Plan

beats.scene: Dara carries a cardboard box out through the glass doors of Marlow Shoes
beats.summary: Marlow Shoes closes, and Dara, aged twenty-nine, leaves with her things in a box.

beats.scene: Dara on a bus by a rainy window, box on her knees
beats.summary: On the bus home she feels empty and does not know what to do next.

beats.scene: Dara in her small kitchen beside the unopened box and cold tea
beats.summary: At home she leaves the box on the floor and sits in the quiet.

beats.scene: Dara sits on her sofa in the dim evening, wiping her eyes
beats.summary: She lets herself cry and does not try to feel better in a hurry.

beats.scene: Dara's phone lights up with cheerful messages from old colleagues
beats.summary: Her old colleagues send hopeful messages, but Dara cannot answer them yet.

beats.scene: Dara lies awake at night while a neighbour's voice tells her to cheer up
beats.summary: For three days she feels everything, and she learns that feelings cannot be hurried.

beats.scene: Dara holds her phone while her sister Leila's name glows on the screen
beats.summary: Her sister Leila calls, and Dara says she is fine when she is not.

beats.scene: Dara stares at the ceiling at dawn, a dark thought circling above her
beats.summary: On the fourth morning she notices a thought that keeps repeating: I am a failure.

beats.scene: Dara looks out of a rainy window at people hurrying under umbrellas
beats.summary: A thought is not always a fact, and a bad day is not a bad life.

beats.scene: Dara opens the window wide and breathes in the cool morning air
beats.summary: She decides to look honestly at what she still has.

beats.scene: Dara writes a list on a notepad beside a steaming mug
beats.summary: Dara makes an honest list of what she still has: her health, her flat, her sister.

beats.scene: Dara counts numbers on a bank statement with a calculator at the table
beats.summary: She counts her savings, and they will last about four months; facing the number shrinks the fear.

beats.scene: Dara writes skills on a page: patient, quick, good with angry customers
beats.summary: She lists what six years of customer orders taught her, and the skills are still hers.

beats.scene: A muscle drawn on a diagram beside a pile of heavy weights
beats.summary: Strength is built by use, much like a muscle, and nobody is simply handed it.

beats.scene: Dara unpacks the box and sets a drooping plant on the windowsill
beats.summary: She unpacks the box at last and waters her plant.

beats.scene: Hugo in a green coat with an old spaniel at a gate
beats.summary: Her neighbour Hugo, a retired firefighter, notices her curtains have been shut for days.

beats.scene: Dara stands in her doorway in a dressing gown, shaking her head
beats.summary: Dara says no to a morning walk, and Hugo says he will knock tomorrow anyway.

beats.scene: Hugo and Dara sit on her front step with two mugs of tea
beats.summary: Hugo explains his rule: one small hard thing each day, however small.

beats.scene: Dara types a short honest message to Mina on her phone
beats.summary: Dara chooses her first hard thing: writing an honest reply to a friend.

beats.scene: Dara and Hugo walk with the slow old dog along a street at dawn
beats.summary: She takes her first ten-minute walk at dawn and comes home feeling a little lighter.

beats.scene: Dara and Hugo walk with Pepper along Alder Road in the cold light
beats.summary: Day after day Dara walks at dawn, and the street slowly becomes familiar again.

beats.scene: Hugo draws a small circle in his notebook and a larger ring around it
beats.summary: Hugo explains that the comfort zone feels safe, but it can shrink if we never leave it.

beats.scene: Dara sits among unopened letters and a silent phone on the sofa
beats.summary: Dara sees that her own circle has been shrinking: she avoids letters, calls and shops.

beats.scene: Dara holds a phone to her ear beside a pile of opened post
beats.summary: Her hard thing is to open the post and phone about a bill.

beats.scene: Dara stands at the edge of a cold swimming pool, thinking
beats.summary: Hugo takes her to the community pool, and she cannot quite make herself get in.

beats.scene: Hugo points to a sign and then to the water, asking a question
beats.summary: Hugo asks whether the water is dangerous or only uncomfortable, and the two are not the same.

beats.scene: Dara gasps in chest-high water, laughing with her arms in the air
beats.summary: She steps in, gasps and finds that she is fine.

beats.scene: Dara holds her hand to her chest with a nervous smile
beats.summary: Before an important call her heart races, and fear and excitement feel much the same in the body.

beats.scene: Dara whispers to herself beside a phone, looking brave
beats.summary: She tries saying I am excited instead of I am scared, which may help some people.

beats.scene: A calendar with fourteen crosses marked in blue pen
beats.summary: After two weeks of small hard things, she can see a pattern of days kept.

beats.scene: Dara lies awake at night with her hand on her fast heart
beats.summary: One night at three in the morning her worries race, and she cannot sleep.

beats.scene: Hugo counts on his fingers while Dara sits upright with closed eyes
beats.summary: Hugo teaches her slow breathing: in for four counts, out for six.

beats.scene: Dara breathes slowly in a chair with her eyes closed
beats.summary: A longer breath out tends to help the body calm down, and she practises it each day.

beats.scene: Dara writes the word nervous on a page and looks calmer
beats.summary: Putting a name to a feeling can make it less strong, and she tries it.

beats.scene: A wave rises and falls on a grey sea seen from a window
beats.summary: Feelings rise and fall like waves, and none of them stays for ever.

beats.scene: Dara looks into a hallway mirror, frowning at herself
beats.summary: She notices how harshly she speaks to herself in her head.

beats.scene: Dara speaks to her reflection with a small awkward smile
beats.summary: She tries speaking to herself as she would to Leila, and it feels strange but helpful.

beats.scene: A page of scribbled worries is folded and placed in a drawer
beats.summary: Writing worries on paper gets them out of her head for a while.

beats.scene: Dara sits at her table in the evening with a timer and a notebook
beats.summary: She sets ten minutes of worry time in the evening and keeps her worries for then.

beats.scene: Dara reads an old page of worries and crosses out most of them
beats.summary: A week later she finds that most of her worries never happened.

beats.scene: Dara works on her laptop at the kitchen table with a pile of notes
beats.summary: Dara updates her CV and sends twelve job applications in one week.

beats.scene: Dara reads an email on her phone with a heavy expression
beats.summary: Her first application is rejected, and it hurts.

beats.scene: Dara sits at a table writing notes next to the rejection email
beats.summary: She allows herself an hour to be sad and then asks what she can improve.

beats.scene: Dara checks an empty inbox beside a cold cup of coffee
beats.summary: More rejections and long silences follow, and she learns that this is normal.

beats.scene: Dara reads a short kind reply on her laptop screen with raised eyebrows
beats.summary: One company answers her request for feedback with a single useful tip.

beats.scene: Dara marks a page of her CV with a pen, adding numbers
beats.summary: She rewrites her CV to show what she achieved, with real numbers.

beats.scene: Hugo and Dara sit across from each other at a kitchen table
beats.summary: Hugo plays the interviewer in his kitchen so that she can practise.

beats.scene: Dara laughs with her hand over her mouth while Hugo grins
beats.summary: She stumbles on the first question, tries again and finds it easier.

beats.scene: Dara in a smart shirt waits on a chair in a bright lobby
beats.summary: Dara is invited to a real interview at Halden Logistics and arrives early.

beats.scene: Dara sits across a desk from two interviewers, answering with open hands
beats.summary: The interview goes well apart from one question she cannot answer, so she says so honestly.

beats.scene: Dara reads an email on her laptop, her shoulders dropping
beats.summary: Halden Logistics chooses someone else, but says she was a close second.

beats.scene: Dara sits on a park bench with her hands on her knees, tired
beats.summary: Dara feels worn out one morning, and she wonders if she has anything left.

beats.scene: Dara walks up a gentle hill while Hugo points ahead with his stick
beats.summary: Hugo says tired does not always mean empty, and they go a little further, listening for real pain.

beats.scene: A bed, a clock and a phone charging across the room
beats.summary: Sleep is the foundation, so she sets a bedtime and leaves her phone across the room.

beats.scene: A bowl of beans and vegetables on a kitchen table
beats.summary: She stops skipping meals and cooks simple dinners of beans, rice and vegetables.

beats.scene: A pair of trainers waiting by a front door at dawn
beats.summary: Movement is the third foundation, and she leaves her trainers by the door.

beats.scene: Dara makes her bed neatly in a bright bedroom
beats.summary: A small morning habit gives her a feeling of order and a first win.

beats.scene: A handwritten card stuck to a mirror listing four morning steps
beats.summary: She writes a short morning routine on a card and sticks it to the mirror.

beats.scene: Dara sits on the edge of her bed in the grey morning, yawning
beats.summary: After a bad night she does the smallest version of her routine, and it still counts.

beats.scene: A poster for a charity ten-kilometre run on a park gate
beats.summary: At the park gate Dara sees a poster for the Riverside Ten, twelve weeks away.

beats.scene: Dara laughs at the poster with a bus pulling away behind her
beats.summary: Dara laughs at the idea, because she cannot even run for a bus.

beats.scene: Hugo and Dara sit on a bench with takeaway tea, looking at the poster
beats.summary: Hugo does not push her, but asks what a good yes would look like.

beats.scene: Dara writes three reasons in a notebook at the kitchen table
beats.summary: She writes her reasons down: not to impress anyone, but to prove something to herself.

beats.scene: Dara signs a charity run entry form at a counter in a sports shop
beats.summary: At Stride Sports Dara signs up for the Riverside Ten, and Jo fits her first running shoes.

beats.scene: Dara talks on the phone while Leila appears on screen, laughing and excited
beats.summary: Dara tells her sister Leila, who promises to bring the children to cheer.

beats.scene: A weekly plan on a fridge with short runs and rest days marked
beats.summary: Hugo helps her make a gradual plan of short runs and walks that builds up slowly.

beats.scene: Hugo holds up a hand, showing a stop sign, in a park
beats.summary: He explains that doing too much too soon is how beginners get hurt.

beats.scene: Dara runs along a park path in worn trainers, red-faced
beats.summary: Her first run lasts two minutes, and she is proud of it.

beats.scene: Dara winces on the stairs, holding the banister, with a grin
beats.summary: The next day her legs are sore, and a rest day is part of the plan.

beats.scene: Dara ticks week one on the fridge plan with a blue pen
beats.summary: Week one is done, and she tells Mina, who sends back a row of cheering faces.

beats.scene: Rain streaks a window while trainers wait by the door
beats.summary: On a wet run day Dara wants to stay in bed with the blankets over her head.

beats.scene: Dara walks slowly in rain with her hood up and a determined face
beats.summary: On hard days she shows up and does less, rather than nothing.

beats.scene: Dara pictures herself running up a hill in a thought bubble
beats.summary: She plans ahead for obstacles with simple if-then plans.

beats.scene: Index cards on the fridge each beginning with the word If
beats.summary: She writes cards for her usual excuses: tired, cold, busy and embarrassed.

beats.scene: A tall jogger passes Dara on the path while she looks at her feet
beats.summary: Dara feels sure that everyone is watching her, but most people are thinking about themselves.

beats.scene: Dara meets Ines, a smiling older runner in a bright cap
beats.summary: On the river path Dara meets Ines, a slow runner who says we are all beginners.

beats.scene: Dara runs steadily by trees, counting her breaths, five minutes on a watch
beats.summary: In week three she runs five minutes without stopping.

beats.scene: Dara runs along the river path at sunrise, light on the water
beats.summary: One morning she enjoys running for the first time, with the river shining beside her.

beats.scene: Dara climbs the stairs of her building two at a time, smiling
beats.summary: She notices that stairs, sleep and moods are all easier than a month ago.

beats.scene: Dara frowns at a calculator and a bank statement at the table
beats.summary: In week four she checks her money, and the old fear comes back.

beats.scene: Dara arrives at Leila's front door as two small children run out
beats.summary: On Sunday Dara visits her sister's family and acts as if everything is fine.

beats.scene: Dara talks to her sister Leila on a sofa, holding a cup
beats.summary: Dara tells Leila how she really feels, and asking for help is not weakness.

beats.scene: Leila listens with her hand on Dara's arm beside a plate of biscuits
beats.summary: Leila does not try to fix everything, but she offers to read Dara's CV and to cook on Sundays.

beats.scene: Dara watches Leila rock a sleepy child and thinks, smiling
beats.summary: Dara realises she would help Leila without thinking less of her, so she can accept help too.

beats.scene: Dara sits among friends around a table laughing together
beats.summary: Supportive friends help us to stay strong, and Dara has dinner with Mina and Tomas.

beats.scene: Dara stands outside a café, politely waving goodbye to a gloomy friend
beats.summary: One friend complains all evening, and Dara learns she can choose how much time to spend with whom.

beats.scene: Dara holds an old exam paper with a red mark in a dusty attic
beats.summary: In Leila's attic Dara finds a maths exam paper she failed at sixteen.

beats.scene: Dara reads old notes at a desk and nods, seeing a lesson
beats.summary: She sees that she never asked for help then, and that she passed the second time after asking.

beats.scene: Dara reads a library book about people who bounce back from hard times
beats.summary: Most people recover from hard times better than they expect, though some need extra help.

beats.scene: Dara watches a sunrise over a river with a small smile
beats.summary: Dara watches the sun rise over the river and feels a quiet hope.

beats.scene: Dara writes three lines in a small notebook at bedtime
beats.summary: Each night she writes three good things from the day, and the first night it is hard.

beats.scene: An open notebook beside a lamp with a pen resting on the page
beats.summary: Writing good things down trains the mind to notice them, though the effect is modest.

beats.scene: A café worker hands Dara a cup while a sparrow hops by her table
beats.summary: She notices a barista's kindness, a sparrow and Pepper's wagging tail.

beats.scene: Dara writes a hard thing and a good thing side by side
beats.summary: She does not hide the bad days, because good things do not cancel the hard ones.

beats.scene: Dara runs through a park under green trees, eight minutes shown on her watch
beats.summary: In week five she runs for eight minutes and feels strong.

beats.scene: Dara runs fast down a hill and twists her ankle at a kerb
beats.summary: In week six she runs too fast downhill and twists her ankle on a kerb.

beats.scene: Hugo holds a bag of frozen peas on Dara's ankle on her sofa
beats.summary: Hugo helps her home, where she rests with her foot up and a cold pack on her ankle.

beats.scene: Dara throws her trainers into the corner of the room, furious
beats.summary: She is furious, because twelve weeks seemed to be slipping away.

beats.scene: Dara lies awake in the dark with her foot raised on a cushion
beats.summary: That night she is sure that the race is over and that she has failed again.

beats.scene: Hugo sits at her table with a mug and a calm face
beats.summary: Hugo says a setback is a bend in the road, not the end of it, and she books the doctor.

beats.scene: A doctor looks at Dara's ankle in a bright clinic room
beats.summary: Dr Anand examines the ankle and finds a mild sprain that needs rest.

beats.scene: Dara sits on the clinic steps with a leaflet and a frowning face
beats.summary: She must rest for about ten days, and resting feels like weakness.

beats.scene: Hugo shows Dara a scar on his knee on the doorstep
beats.summary: Hugo tells her that he once ran on an injury, made it worse and lost a whole season.

beats.scene: Dara swims slowly in a calm pool while the ankle stays rested
beats.summary: While her ankle heals she finds another way to stay active: swimming.

beats.scene: Dara floats on her back in the pool, smiling at the ceiling lights
beats.summary: She remembers how afraid she was of this cold water, and now she floats in it.

beats.scene: Dara draws letters in the air with her foot on a chair
beats.summary: She does the gentle ankle exercises she was shown, every single day.

beats.scene: Dara sits at the kitchen table at night, hands over her face
beats.summary: Doubt returns at night, and she thinks I can't do this.

beats.scene: Dara writes I can do the next step on a card
beats.summary: She changes I can't into I can do the next step.

beats.scene: Dara ties her shoelaces on a doorstep in the early light
beats.summary: She looks only at the next step in front of her, not the whole mountain.

beats.scene: Dara and Hugo walk and jog gently along a flat path
beats.summary: The ankle is better, and they make a new plan to walk and run the whole race.

beats.scene: Dara sits at the table with a nearly empty bank statement and a phone
beats.summary: Her savings are nearly gone, and she faces the number honestly.

beats.scene: Hugo and Dara talk on a bench with tea, looking at a grey sky
beats.summary: Hugo says that a job that is less than you hoped for can be a bridge.

beats.scene: Dara listens to a phone call from a recruitment agency at her kitchen table
beats.summary: An agency offers a three-month office job at Brightwell Supplies, with lower pay than before.

beats.scene: Dara shakes hands with a manager in a small bright office
beats.summary: Dara swallows her pride and accepts the temporary job.

beats.scene: Dara looks lost in a new office with unfamiliar desks around her
beats.summary: On the first day she is a beginner again and feels clumsy.

beats.scene: A colleague named Kofi shows Dara a screen with a patient smile
beats.summary: She decides to accept being a beginner, and she asks questions; Kofi helps her.

beats.scene: Dara stares at a screen with her hand over her mouth
beats.summary: Dara sends an order to the wrong address, and she owns the mistake at once.

beats.scene: Dara and Hugo laugh over tea, a fire helmet on a shelf
beats.summary: Hugo says every firefighter was once a rookie who tripped over the hose.

beats.scene: Dara calmly speaks on the phone while Ms Barrow watches from a desk
beats.summary: Her old skill of calming angry customers shines, and Ms Barrow notices.

beats.scene: Dara runs gently along a river path at dawn, a bag on her shoulder
beats.summary: At the end of the first week she runs at dawn before work.

beats.scene: Ms Barrow talks to Dara across a desk, holding a printed page
beats.summary: Ms Barrow asks Dara to explain her new order checks at Friday's team meeting.

beats.scene: Dara stands before a small meeting with notes in shaking hands
beats.summary: Dara's hands shake at the very thought, and she wants to say no.

beats.scene: Dara writes five short points on index cards at her kitchen table
beats.summary: She says yes, then writes five short points on cards and practises aloud.

beats.scene: Hugo and Pepper listen while Dara practises her talk in his kitchen
beats.summary: Hugo listens to her practise and says that nerves show she cares.

beats.scene: Dara sits in bed breathing slowly with a card in her hand
beats.summary: The night before, she breathes slowly and makes an if-then plan for losing her place.

beats.scene: Dara breathes slowly at a lectern with a single card in her hand
beats.summary: She begins with just one sentence, which is all she needs to start.

beats.scene: Dara's hands tremble on a card while her voice stays steady
beats.summary: Her hands shake, but her voice stays steady.

beats.scene: Dara pauses and looks down at a card in front of a quiet room
beats.summary: She loses her place, pauses, finds it again and carries on.

beats.scene: Dara finishes speaking and her colleagues clap politely
beats.summary: The talk goes fine, not perfectly, and she survives.

beats.scene: Kofi smiles at Dara with a thumbs up beside a printed label
beats.summary: Kofi tells her that one of her ideas has already helped him.

beats.scene: Dara writes a list on a sheet of paper at the kitchen table
beats.summary: Dara writes a list of all the hard things she has done since March.

beats.scene: A short list of achievements stuck to a fridge door
beats.summary: She keeps the list on the fridge as proof of her strength, not as a boast.

beats.scene: Dara reads the fridge list at night with a mug, the lamp low
beats.summary: On a bad day she reads the list, because evidence is stronger than a mood.

beats.scene: Dara adds a new line to the fridge list with a pen
beats.summary: She adds one new line every week, even for small things.

beats.scene: Dara and Ines jog and walk beside the river in the morning
beats.summary: In week ten Dara and Ines walk and run six kilometres along the river.

beats.scene: Dara tries on shoes and socks while Jo shows a water bottle
beats.summary: At Stride Sports, Jo reminds her not to try anything new on race day.

beats.scene: Dara pins a paper number to her shirt in front of a mirror
beats.summary: Her race number arrives, and she pins it to her shirt and feels both fear and excitement.

beats.scene: Dara frowns on a bench, picturing herself last in a long line of runners
beats.summary: Dara worries that she will finish last, and Hugo says that last still means finished.

beats.scene: Dara walks and runs eight kilometres, a watch showing the distance
beats.summary: On Sunday she covers eight kilometres, the farthest she has ever gone, and the ankle holds.

beats.scene: Leila's two children paint a banner with bright letters on the floor
beats.summary: Leila sends a photo of the children painting a banner for the finish line.

beats.scene: A weather map with dark clouds on a kitchen radio and a calendar
beats.summary: Week eleven begins with a forecast of heavy rain and wind.

beats.scene: Dara steps up and down on the stairs of her building, laughing
beats.summary: Her if-then plan for storms is to train on the stairs, and she does.

beats.scene: Dara runs along a street in heavy rain with a grim smile
beats.summary: On Thursday there is rain but no thunder, and she runs slowly anyway.

beats.scene: Dara jumps into a puddle, soaked and laughing, hood fallen back
beats.summary: Soaked to the skin, she laughs at a puddle and discovers she likes the rain.

beats.scene: Dara in a blanket with a tissue and a cup of tea
beats.summary: The next day she has a sniffly cold and rests, listening to her body.

beats.scene: A training plan on a fridge with the last week's runs short
beats.summary: In the last week the plan asks for less running, and she must trust her training.

beats.scene: Dara and Hugo eat pasta at his kitchen table with Pepper beneath it
beats.summary: Hugo cooks pasta, and he tells her about running a race in his full firefighter kit.

beats.scene: Race kit laid out neatly on a bedroom chair under a lamp
beats.summary: The night before, she lays out her kit and her number, and her nerves rise.

beats.scene: Dara lies in bed writing two words in a notebook by a small lamp
beats.summary: She cannot sleep, so she names her feelings: excited and scared, and both are allowed.

beats.scene: Dara and Hugo stand at the gate with Pepper in the dark before dawn
beats.summary: At five the alarm rings, and Hugo is already at her gate, ready to walk to the bus.

beats.scene: Dara stands among hundreds of runners at a starting line at dawn
beats.summary: On race day Dara is nervous at the starting line outside the Town Hall.

beats.scene: A woman in a food bank T-shirt smiles in a crowd of runners
beats.summary: She sees runners of every age and size, and she feels part of something larger.

beats.scene: Hugo hugs Dara beside the barriers with Pepper wagging beside him
beats.summary: Hugo gives her one last piece of advice: start slowly, and run your own race.

beats.scene: A starting horn is raised above a sea of heads in the early light
beats.summary: The horn sounds, and she starts slowly on purpose.

beats.scene: Dara runs among a fast crowd, glancing at her watch with a frown
beats.summary: In the first kilometre she goes too fast, remembers the plan and slows down.

beats.scene: Dara runs beside the river as strangers clap from a bridge
beats.summary: By the third kilometre she finds a rhythm, and strangers clap from the bridge.

beats.scene: Leila, Samir and Nadia hold the banner high beside the road
beats.summary: At the five-kilometre mark Leila and the children cheer and wave the banner.

beats.scene: Dara slows with a hand on her thigh, listening to her ankle
beats.summary: At six kilometres her legs are heavy, and she asks whether it is pain or effort.

beats.scene: Dara walks beside the road while other runners pass her
beats.summary: At seven kilometres she wants to stop, so she walks.

beats.scene: Dara points to a lamp post ahead and begins to run again
beats.summary: She drinks, picks a lamp post, runs to it and then picks another.

beats.scene: Ines in her bright cap jogs beside Dara on a crowded road
beats.summary: At eight kilometres Ines appears at her side, encouraging her: nearly there.

beats.scene: Dara runs through the gates of Linden Park between lines of clapping people
beats.summary: At nine kilometres she runs through the park gates between rows of clapping people.

beats.scene: Dara runs with her eyes half closed, remembering a box and a bus
beats.summary: In the last kilometre she remembers the box, the bus and the cold tea, and how far she has come.

beats.scene: A finishing arch glows at the end of a long park path
beats.summary: She sees the finishing arch and hears the crowd roaring.

beats.scene: Dara crosses the finish line with her arms in the air, crying and smiling
beats.summary: Dara finishes the race; it is not fast, but she has done it.

beats.scene: A volunteer places a medal around Dara's neck and wraps a blanket round her
beats.summary: A volunteer gives her a medal and a silver blanket.

beats.scene: Hugo, Leila and the children hug Dara beside Pepper
beats.summary: Hugo, Leila and the children find her, and everybody hugs.

beats.summary: She does not spiral, because one bad day is not a bad life, and she apologises.

beats.summary: She starts a short review every Sunday to protect her habits.

beats.summary: Leila is exhausted, and Dara listens to her as Leila once listened to Dara.

Hugo cooks pasta, and he tells Dara about a race in his work clothes.
The night before, Dara puts out her clothes, and she feels very nervous.
Dara cannot sleep, so she writes: excited and scared, and both are fine.

In the first kilometre, Dara goes too fast, so she slows down.

At five kilometres, Leila and the children wave a big banner.

A kind helper puts a medal around Dara's neck and gives her a blanket.

Hugo, Leila and the children find Dara, and everyone hugs her.

That night, Dara adds a new line to her list: I finished the race.

Hugo says, it is normal after a big goal, and it will pass.
Dara breathes slowly, writes the word flat and goes for a walk.

Dara picks a new goal and signs up for an evening class.

Dara says sorry to Kofi, and one bad day is not a bad life.
Every Sunday, Dara looks back over her week to keep her habits.

Hugo needs an operation on his knee, so Dara walks Pepper each morning.
A new neighbour, Ben, sits on the stairs with his head down.

B1B2: Dara is twenty-nine, and today is the last day at Marlow Shoes, where she has worked for six years. She puts her mug, her plant and a photograph into one cardboard box and walks out.
On the bus home, Dara holds the box on her knees and watches the rain run down the window. She has no plan for tomorrow, and the strange thing is that she feels almost nothing at all.
Back in her flat, Dara puts the box on the kitchen floor and cannot bring herself to open it. She sits at the table beside a cup of tea that went cold hours ago.
That evening the feelings finally arrive, and Dara cries on the sofa until her head aches. She does not try to cheer herself up, because she suspects it would only push the sadness down.
Her phone fills with messages from old colleagues, and most of them say that everything will be fine. Dara reads them all, but she cannot think of a single honest thing to answer.
For three days Dara sleeps badly, eats little and lets herself feel whatever comes. A neighbour tells her to cheer up, but Dara knows that feelings cannot be hurried.
On the third night her sister Leila rings, and Dara says that she is fine. Leila waits a moment and then says, quietly, that she does not sound fine at all.
On the fourth morning Dara wakes before dawn and notices a thought that keeps repeating: I am a failure. It sounds so certain that she almost believes it.
Dara looks out at people hurrying through the rain under their umbrellas, and she begins to wonder about the thought. It is only a thought, not a fact, and one bad day is not the same as a bad life.
Dara opens the window and lets the cool morning air into the flat for the first time in days. She makes a cup of tea, finds a pen and decides to look honestly at what she still has.
Dara sits at the kitchen table and writes down what she still has. The list is longer than she expected, because it holds her health, her flat, her sister Leila and a head full of useful knowledge.

Next she opens her bank account and counts her savings with a calculator, even though her stomach turns over. They will last about four months, and somehow a number she can see frightens her less than a fog she cannot.

On a clean page Dara writes what six years of customer orders have taught her, and the list is long. She is patient, quick with figures and calm with angry strangers, and none of these skills closed down with the company.

While she waits for the kettle, Dara thinks about people she knows who are strong, and she realises that none of them was handed it. Strength is built through use, much like a muscle, and it grows slowly through effort and rest.
At last Dara opens the cardboard box and sets her mug on the shelf and her photograph by the bed. The plant is drooping badly, so she gives it a long drink of water and moves it onto the windowsill.

On the sixth day a man in a green coat stops at her gate with an old spaniel on a lead. He is Hugo, the retired firefighter from next door, and he says he has noticed that her curtains have stayed closed all week.

Dara stands in the doorway in her dressing gown and says that she does not feel like walking. Hugo only smiles, nods and tells her that he will knock again tomorrow at seven, whether she likes it or not.
He sits on her front step with a mug of tea and tells her the one rule he lives by. Every day, do one small thing you would rather not do, and do it before you can talk yourself out of it.

All afternoon Dara thinks about what her small hard thing could be. She decides to answer Mina's message honestly, and after four attempts she writes that she is scared but that she is getting through each day.

At seven the next morning Hugo knocks, and Dara goes out in her coat while the street is still grey and quiet. They walk for ten slow minutes behind his old dog, and she returns home feeling a little lighter than she has for days.

Every morning at seven Hugo knocks, and the two of them walk along Alder Road behind slow old Pepper. The street slowly becomes familiar again, with its cat on the wall, its smell of bread and its neighbours opening their curtains.

One morning Hugo stops under a lamp post and draws a small circle in his notebook, with a larger ring around it. The small circle is the comfort zone, he says, and it feels safe, but it grows smaller if we never step outside it.

Back at home Dara looks at the unopened letters on the sofa and the silent phone beside them. She realises that her circle has shrunk since she lost her job, because she avoids letters, calls and even the corner shop.

She decides that today's hard thing is to open every letter and to ring the gas company about a bill that looks wrong. The call lasts six minutes, the mistake is fixed, and Dara puts the phone down feeling taller than she has for weeks.

On Saturday Hugo takes her to the community pool in Linden Park, where he swims slowly every week. Dara stands on the edge in her swimming costume, looking at the pale blue water, and she cannot make herself get in.

Hugo points to the lifeguard and then the water, and asks her a question: is it dangerous, or only uncomfortable? He says that most of the things we avoid are the second kind, and the two are easy to confuse.

Dara sits down, slides off the edge and gasps as the cold water reaches her chest. She waves her arms and laughs out loud, and she realises that nothing dreadful has happened and that she is perfectly fine.

Later that week Dara has to ring a company about a job, and her heart starts to race as she dials. Hugo has told her that fear and excitement feel very similar in the body, with the same fast heartbeat and the same buzzing hands.

He suggests that she tell herself, I am excited, instead of I am scared, before she speaks. Dara feels a little silly, but she tries it, and her voice comes out steadier than she expected, though she knows it is not magic.

On the kitchen wall Dara has pinned a calendar, and she puts a blue cross on every day she has kept her promise. After two weeks there are fourteen crosses in a row, and she is surprised by how much she wants to keep the line unbroken.

At three o'clock one morning Dara wakes with her heart pounding and a long list of worries running through her mind. She turns over, checks the clock twice and knows that she will not get back to sleep.
On their next walk she tells Hugo about the sleepless night, and he stops on the pavement to show her something. He counts on his fingers and tells her to breathe in for four counts and out for six.

He explains that a longer breath out tends to slow the heart and calm the body, although it is not a cure for anything. Dara practises in her chair every afternoon with her eyes closed, and after a few days she can feel the difference.

When her stomach tightens before a phone call, Dara takes a pen and writes the word nervous on a page. Hugo has told her that naming a feeling can make it less strong, and she is surprised to find that it seems to work.

She begins to list the feelings she has each day: ashamed, hopeful, angry, bored, and then ashamed again. Hugo tells her that feelings rise and fall like waves, so none of them stays for ever, even the ones that feel endless.

One evening Dara catches sight of herself in the hall mirror and hears what she has been saying inside her head. Stupid, useless, hopeless, she thinks, and she realises that she would never speak that way to anyone she cared about.

She decides to try an experiment and talks to her reflection in the voice she would use for her sister Leila. It feels strange, and her cheeks go pink, but the sharp edge of the thought really does seem to soften.

Another night Dara cannot stop the worries from circling, so she writes every one on a sheet of paper. She folds it twice, puts it in the kitchen drawer and finds that her head feels lighter and a little less crowded.

After a few days she makes herself a rule of ten minutes of worry time at six each evening, with a timer and a notebook. If a worry arrives at another hour, she tells it kindly that it will have to wait until six.

A week later Dara reads the old page of worries and crosses out most of them, because nearly all have never happened. She knows that some worries are real and some days really are hard, but she is learning to tell the difference.

With Hugo's old pen and her own good sense, Dara updates her CV and sends out twelve applications in one week. She hits the button each time with a small flutter of hope, and then she closes the laptop and goes for a walk.

The first reply arrives on Thursday morning, and it is a short, polite email that begins with the words thank you for your interest. Dara reads it three times, and each time the word unfortunately feels like a small punch.
She gives herself one hour to be disappointed, with a cup of tea, and then she takes a pen and a clean page. Instead of asking what is wrong with her, she asks what she could improve next time.

Over the next fortnight there are three more refusals, and most of the other companies simply never reply. Hugo tells her that this is normal, and that a long silence usually says more about a busy company than about the person who applied.

Dara decides to be brave and asks one company whether they could tell her why she was not chosen. To her surprise a person writes back within two days, and the answer is kind and short, with one useful tip.

The tip is that her CV lists her duties but never says what she achieved, so Dara rewrites it with numbers. She cut the errors in customer orders by a third, and she answered about forty calls a day, and now it says so.

On Sunday evening Hugo puts on his reading glasses and plays the interviewer at his kitchen table, with a clipboard and a very serious face. His first question is, tell me about yourself, and Dara's mind goes completely blank.

She stumbles through an answer, and Hugo laughs kindly and tells her to start again. By the fourth attempt she has found a short story about her six years at Marlow Shoes, and the words come out much more easily.

A week later Halden Logistics invites her to an interview, and she arrives twenty minutes early in her best shirt. Sitting in the bright lobby with her notes on her knee, she breathes out for six counts and tells herself that she is excited.

The interview goes well, except for one question about a computer system that she has never used. Instead of pretending, she says that she does not know it but that she learns quickly, and she walks out with her head high.

The email from Halden Logistics arrives on Monday morning, and it says that they have chosen someone with more experience. They add that Dara was a close second, which is kind, but she still feels her shoulders drop.

A few days later Dara sits down on a bench in Linden Park in the middle of their walk and cannot go on. She is tired in a way that sleep does not seem to fix, and she wonders whether she has anything left at all.

Hugo does not hurry her, and after a while he says that tired does not always mean empty. They climb the gentle hill a little further together, and he tells her to listen for real pain, which is different from effort.

That night Dara looks at how she has been living, and she decides to build on three plain foundations, beginning with sleep. She picks a bedtime, switches off the lamp and leaves her phone charging in the other room.
The second foundation is food, and she stops skipping lunch and eating biscuits for dinner. She cooks simple meals of beans, rice and vegetables, and she notices that her afternoons feel steadier.

The third foundation is movement, and Dara places her old trainers beside the front door so that she cannot miss them. Hugo has told her that it is easier to begin when the next step is already sitting in front of you.
Every morning, before she does anything else, Dara makes her bed with the corners pulled straight. It takes one minute, and it gives her a small feeling of order and a first win before breakfast.

She writes a short morning routine on a card and sticks it to the bathroom mirror: water, bed, trainers, one hard thing. The card is not clever, but it saves her from having to decide everything while she is still half asleep.

After a bad night Dara wakes up feeling heavy and cross, and she wants to stay under the blankets. She does the smallest version of her routine instead, a glass of water and a made bed, and she tells herself that it still counts.

On the way home from the park Dara stops at the gate, where a bright poster has been tied to the railings. It announces the Riverside Ten, a charity run of ten kilometres in exactly twelve weeks, and she smiles and shakes her head.
Dara laughs out loud at the poster, because she cannot even run for a bus without losing her breath. Behind her a bus pulls away from the stop, which seems to prove the point.
That evening she mentions the poster to Hugo, and he does not push her either way. He only asks what would make this a good yes for her, and then he waits, as he always does, for her real answer.

At the kitchen table Dara writes down three reasons in her notebook, and she is surprised by what she finds. She does not want to impress anyone, because she wants to prove something to herself, and the money will help the local food bank.

On Saturday she goes into Stride Sports and signs the entry form at the counter before her courage can run away. Jo, the assistant, watches her walk up and down the shop and chooses a pair of running shoes that fit her feet properly.
Dara rings her sister Leila, half expecting her to laugh, but Leila squeals so loudly that Dara holds the phone away. She promises to bring both children to cheer at the finish line, with a banner.
Hugo helps her to make a gradual plan, with short runs mixed with walking, and rest days between them. They pin it to the fridge, and Dara is amazed at how small the first week looks.

Hugo explains that most beginners get hurt by doing too much too soon, not by doing too little. The plan builds slowly on purpose, and a rest day is not laziness but a way of letting the body get stronger.

On Monday morning Dara runs for two minutes along the park path in her new shoes, and her face goes the colour of a tomato. She stops, bends over and laughs between her gasps, because it is the longest run she has done since school.

The next morning her legs are so sore that she goes down the stairs sideways and holds the banister with both hands. Hugo tells her that this soreness is normal after something new, and she is glad that today is a rest day.

By Sunday Dara has finished week one of the plan, and she puts a neat blue tick on the fridge. She sends a message to Mina, who replies at once with a row of cheering faces and a request for photographs.
On Thursday the rain beats against the window, and the plan on the fridge says it is a run day. Dara pulls the blankets over her head and tells herself that nobody would blame her for staying in.

Instead she puts on her yellow jacket and pulls up the hood, and she decides to do less rather than nothing. She walks for ten minutes through the rain, and when she gets home she feels as proud as if she had run a mile.

Hugo tells her that people keep their promises more often when they plan for the difficult moments in advance. He calls it an if-then plan, such as if it rains, then I wear my yellow jacket and go out for ten minutes.

That evening Dara writes cards for her four favourite excuses, which are tired, cold, busy and embarrassed, and she pins them to the fridge. Each card begins with the word if, and each ends with a small, sensible action that she can actually do.

On Saturday a tall runner overtakes Dara on the path, and she keeps her eyes on her feet, sure that everyone is staring. Hugo says that people usually spend their time thinking about themselves, not about the red-faced beginner who is puffing along behind them.

Further along the river path a smiling woman in a bright cap waves and slows down to run beside Dara for a moment. Her name is Ines, she is in her sixties, and she says cheerfully that every runner on the path was once a beginner.

In week three the plan asks Dara to run for five minutes without stopping, which she has never done. She counts her breaths, keeps her shoulders loose and finds, when the watch finally beeps, that she could have gone on a little longer.

On a still morning she reaches the river path just as the sun lifts over the trees and sets the water on fire. For the first time she is not counting the seconds, because she is enjoying the quiet rhythm of her own feet.

One day she realises that she is climbing the stairs of her building two at a time without thinking about it. She is sleeping better, her mood is steadier, and she knows these changes are small and have come one morning at a time.

At the end of week four Dara sits down with a calculator and her bank statement and does the sum she has been avoiding. She has about six weeks of savings left, and the old fear comes rushing back into her stomach.
On Sunday Dara goes to her sister's house, where Samir and Nadia hurl themselves at her legs. She smiles, hands over the biscuits she has brought and tells everyone that she is doing wonderfully.

After lunch Leila finds her alone in the kitchen with a cup of tea, and she simply sits down beside her. This time Dara does not say she is fine, and she admits that she is frightened about money and feels useless.

Leila does not try to fix everything or tell her that things will be fine, but she listens with her hand on Dara's arm. Then she offers to read Dara's CV and to cook an extra dinner on Sundays, and Dara accepts both.

Watching Leila rock a sleepy child, Dara thinks that she would help her sister at any hour of the day without thinking less of her. If that is true, then perhaps asking for help is not a weakness, and it might even be a kind of strength.

On Friday Mina and Tomas come for dinner, and the three of them laugh until the plates are cold. Dara notices that she feels stronger after an evening with people who are glad she is there, and she decides to see them more.

Another friend, Gareth, spends a whole coffee complaining about everything, and Dara goes home feeling drained. She can choose how she spends her time, so she kindly tells him that she needs a different kind of talk.

While helping Leila to tidy the attic, Dara finds an old exam paper with a large red mark across the top. It is the maths exam she failed at sixteen, and she remembers crying in the toilets and deciding that she was simply bad at numbers.

She reads her old notes and sees what she could not see then, that she never asked her teacher for any help. She did ask the next term and passed the second time, so the paper holds a lesson and not a life sentence.

At the library Dara borrows a book about how people cope with hard times, and she reads that most people recover better than they expect. The writer is careful to add that some people need extra support, and that asking for it is wise and not shameful.

One morning Dara runs to the river and stops on the bridge to watch the sun rise over the water. She is out of breath and her shoes are wet, and for the first time in months she feels a small, steady hope.
Every night before bed Dara writes three good things from the day in a small notebook. On the first night she stares at the page and can only think of toast, a dry pavement and a text from Mina.

Hugo tells her that the point is not to be falsely cheerful but to train the mind to notice what is already there. The effect is modest, and not everyone feels it, but it costs nothing and takes only two minutes.

Over the next few weeks Dara begins to notice small things as she goes through the day. A café worker remembers her name, a sparrow hops onto her table, and Pepper's tail wags as though she were a film star.

On other pages she also writes down the hard things, because she does not want to pretend that the bad days have disappeared. Good things do not cancel the hard ones, but they do remind her that a hard day is never the whole story.

In week five the plan asks for eight minutes of running, and Dara does it on the park path under the green trees. When the watch beeps she is breathing hard but smiling, and for the first time she thinks that she might really finish.

In week six, Dara feels so strong that she runs too fast down the hill, and her foot catches the edge of a kerb. She feels something twist in her ankle and sits down hard on the pavement, with tears of pain and surprise in her eyes.
Hugo, who is walking behind her with Pepper, helps her to her feet and half carries her home. He sits her on the sofa with her foot up on a cushion and holds a bag of frozen peas against her ankle.

When he has gone, Dara throws one of her trainers across the room, and it bounces off the wall and lands in the laundry basket. She is furious with herself, because twelve weeks of work seemed to be slipping away.
That night she lies awake with her foot raised on a pile of pillows, certain that the race is over. The old voice in her head says, I told you so, and she cannot find the strength to answer it.

Next morning Hugo brings two mugs of tea and says that a setback is a bend in the road, not an ending. He tells her that the first step is to find out what is wrong, and she rings the doctor and books an appointment.

Dr Anand turns Dara's ankle gently from side to side and asks her to walk across the room. She says it is a mild sprain, that rest is the best medicine now, and that a physiotherapist can help if it does not improve.

Outside on the clinic steps Dara reads the leaflet, which tells her to rest for about ten days before she runs again. Resting feels like weakness to her, and she cannot help thinking that everyone else is getting ahead.
That evening Hugo lifts his trouser leg on her doorstep and shows her a long, pale scar on his knee. Years ago he ran on an injury because he was too proud to stop, and he lost an entire season.

Dara decides that resting does not have to mean doing nothing, so she goes to the community pool, where swimming does not hurt her ankle. She swims slowly and steadily, and she is glad to find another way to keep moving.

One afternoon she floats on her back in the middle of the pool, looking up at the lights on the ceiling. She remembers how afraid she was of this water on the first day, and she smiles because it now feels like a friend.

At home she does the gentle exercises that Dr Anand showed her, like drawing the alphabet in the air with her foot. It is boring and a little silly, but she does it every day, because the ankle will heal faster if she looks after it.

One night, when the flat is quiet and the plan on the fridge seems like a joke, doubt comes back. Dara puts her hands over her face and whispers that she cannot do this, and she means it with her whole heart.

Then she remembers something that Hugo told her about the words we use, and she takes out a card and a pen. She crosses out the words I can't and writes I can do the next step, and she sticks the card over her bed.

In the morning she looks only at the one thing in front of her, which is tying her shoelaces on the doorstep. She has learned that no one climbs a whole mountain at once, and that you only ever take the next step.

Ten days later Dr Anand says the ankle is much better, and Dara is allowed to start again, gently. Hugo helps her make a new plan, because the aim is now to finish the Riverside Ten, not to finish fast.

At the end of the month Dara looks at her bank statement, and the number at the bottom is almost zero. She feels the old fear in her stomach, but she makes herself look at it for a full minute instead of closing the page.

Hugo listens to her worries on a bench in the park, and he does not tell her that everything is fine. He says that a job that is less than you hoped for can still be a bridge, because it carries you across to somewhere better.

On Friday an agency telephones with an offer of three months in the office of Brightwell Supplies. The work is less interesting than her old job, and the pay is lower, and Dara feels her pride rise up like a wall.

She sits with the offer for one night, writes the good and the bad on a page and finds that the good side is longer. In the morning she says yes, and when she shakes hands with her new manager, Ms Barrow, she is smiling.

On her first day at Brightwell the desks are unfamiliar, the computer system is strange and everyone seems to know exactly what they are doing. Dara has not been a beginner for six years, and she feels clumsy and a little foolish.

She decides to accept that she is a beginner, because there is no other way to stop being one. She asks questions all day, and Kofi at the next desk answers each one with a smile and never makes her feel stupid.

On Thursday Dara sends an order to the wrong address, and her stomach drops when she sees the mistake on the screen. She walks straight to Ms Barrow, explains what happened and offers a plan to put it right, and the order is corrected within the hour.

That evening she tells Hugo about her mistake over tea in his kitchen, where an old fire helmet sits on a shelf. He laughs warmly and says that every firefighter was once a rookie who tripped over the hose and that no one ever forgot it.

On Friday an angry customer rings with a problem, and Dara answers in the calm voice that she used for six years. She listens, repeats the problem back, offers a solution and ends the call with thanks, and across the room Ms Barrow nods slowly.

By the end of the first week Dara is tired, but she finds that the job is not as bad as she feared. On Saturday she runs gently along the river at dawn, and her first pay cheque is coming at the end of the month.
On Tuesday Ms Barrow asks Dara to explain her new order checks to the whole team at the Friday meeting. Dara says that of course she can, and then she walks back to her desk feeling slightly sick.

All afternoon she imagines herself standing at the front, with twenty faces looking at her and her hands shaking. She wants to go back to Ms Barrow and say no, and the wish is so strong that it almost frightens her.

Instead, she tells herself that she can say yes now and be afraid at the same time. That evening she writes five short points on index cards, and she practises the talk aloud at the kitchen table until she knows it well.
On Wednesday she practises in Hugo's kitchen, with Pepper as her only audience, and Hugo listens with his arms folded. He says that nerves show she cares, and that even the best speakers feel them.

On Thursday night Dara lies in bed and breathes in for four counts and out for six until her shoulders drop. She also makes an if-then plan: if I lose my place, then I will stop, look at my card and take one breath.

On Friday she stands at the front of the meeting room with a single card in her hand, and for a second she cannot speak. Then she remembers what Hugo said, and she begins with just one sentence: today I want to show you three small changes.
Her hands are trembling so much that the card shakes like a leaf. She tells herself that this is only her body being excited, and her voice comes out steady and clear.

Halfway through the talk her mind goes blank and she loses her place, and the room becomes very quiet. She stops, looks down at her card, takes one slow breath and finds her place again, and nobody seems to mind at all.
When she says her last sentence, her colleagues clap politely, and Ms Barrow gives her a small nod. The talk was not perfect and it was not brilliant, but it was fine, and she survived it.

Kofi comes over holding a new label and says that her idea saved him an hour that morning. Dara feels warmth spread through her chest, because someone has found her work useful, and that matters more than the applause.

On Sunday evening Dara sits at the kitchen table and writes a list of every hard thing she has done since March. It includes the gas company call, the cold pool, the interview, the first run and the talk at work, and it fills a whole page.

She sticks the list to the fridge, and she tells herself that it is not there to make her proud but to be proof. When she feels weak, the page will tell her what she has already done, and a list cannot be argued with.

On Tuesday evening Dara has a bad day, with a mistake at work and a long grey mood that follows her home. She reads the list slowly in front of the fridge, and it reminds her that a mood is not evidence.
She makes a rule of adding one new line every week, even for small things. This week she adds the words I asked Kofi for help, because the old Dara would have hidden the problem rather than ask.

In week ten Dara meets Ines on the river path, and the two of them walk and run six kilometres together at a chatting pace. Ines tells her stories about her own first race, in which she finished second from last and was thrilled about it.
At Stride Sports Jo helps her to choose some socks and a small water bottle for the race. She reminds Dara never to try anything new on race day, because even a good new shoe can rub on a long run.
On Wednesday her race number arrives in the post, a white square printed with the numbers 1127. She pins it to her top in front of the mirror, and her stomach flips with fear and excitement at once.

That night she lies awake worrying that she will come in last, with everyone else long gone and the finish line empty. She tells Hugo the next morning, and he says that last place still means someone finished, and so many people never start.

On Sunday Dara and Hugo set out along the river, and she walks and runs eight kilometres, the farthest she has ever gone. Her ankle holds up, her breathing stays calm and she finishes with tired legs and a huge smile.

That evening Leila sends a photo of Samir and Nadia on the floor, painting a banner in large wobbly letters. It says GO AUNTIE DARA, and Dara looks at the picture for a long time with a lump in her throat.
At the start of week eleven the radio warns of heavy rain and strong winds, and Dara's heart sinks. She looks at the plan on the fridge and decides that she needs a storm plan of her own.

Her if-then card says that in dangerous weather she will train indoors, so she steps up and down the stairs for twenty minutes. She feels silly at first, but by the end she is out of breath and laughing, and the neighbour on the landing waves.

On Thursday the rain is heavy, but there is no thunder and no lightning, and Dara decides it is safe to go out. She pulls on her yellow jacket and runs slowly along the empty street with a grim little smile on her face.

Halfway round the park she steps in a puddle so deep that the water goes over her shoe, and her hood falls back. Instead of being cross, she starts to laugh, and she is surprised to find that she rather likes the rain.

The next day she wakes up with a sore throat and a runny nose, and she knows she should not push herself today. She stays in with tea and a blanket, and she tells herself that listening to her body is part of training.
In the last week the plan asks her to run much less, so that her legs are fresh on race day. It feels wrong to do less now, but Hugo says that the real work is done and that she must trust it.

Two days before the race Hugo cooks a huge pot of pasta, and they eat it at his kitchen table with Pepper under the chair. He tells her about running a charity race in his full firefighter kit and finishing so hot that he could hardly speak.
On Saturday evening Dara lays out her top, her number, her shoes and her water bottle on the bedroom chair. She checks the list three times, and as she does so her nerves begin to rise.
She cannot sleep, so she takes her notebook and writes two words in the lamplight: excited and scared. She lets both be true, and she remembers that a feeling named is a feeling that is less strong.
At five o'clock the alarm rings in the dark, and Dara dresses quietly and drinks a glass of water. When she opens the door, Hugo is already at her gate with Pepper, ready to walk her to the bus.
On race day the square by the Town Hall is full of runners, and Dara stands among them at dawn. Her stomach flutters, her hands are cold and she cannot remember whether she is excited or terrified.

She looks around and sees people of every age, shape and speed, some in costumes and some in food bank T-shirts. Nobody is looking at her, and the thought that all of them were once beginners makes her feel part of something larger.
Hugo walks her to the barriers with Pepper beside him, and he gives her one last piece of advice. Start slowly, he says, and run your own race, because the others are running theirs.
A voice counts down from ten, and a horn sounds over the heads of the crowd. Dara takes a deep breath and starts slowly on purpose, shuffling forward with the others until the crowd begins to thin.

In the first kilometre the excitement carries her along, and she realises that she is running much faster than the plan. She remembers what she promised herself, slows down to a gentle pace and lets a group of runners go ahead.

By the third kilometre she has found a steady rhythm, with the river shining on her left and the road smooth under her feet. People are clapping from the bridge, and a small boy holds out his hand to give her a high five.

At the five-kilometre mark she hears her name, and there are Leila, Samir and Nadia on the pavement holding the banner high. Dara waves, laughs and cries at the same time, and the shouting carries her along for another long stretch.
At six kilometres her legs have turned heavy, and a small twinge appears in her ankle. She slows down and asks herself the question that Hugo taught her: is this pain, or is it only effort?

At seven kilometres her mind begins to make a very reasonable case for stopping, and everything inside her wants to quit. She does not fight it, so she walks beside the road while other runners pass her, and she feels the old shame rise.

She drinks some water, breathes out slowly for a count of six and chooses a lamp post a short way ahead. She runs to it, and when she reaches it she picks another, and then another, one lamp post at a time.

At eight kilometres she is dragging her feet, and her breathing is loud in her own ears. Then a bright cap appears at her shoulder, and Ines says cheerfully that they are nearly there and will go together.

At nine kilometres the road turns into the gates of Linden Park, and both sides of the path are lined with clapping people. Some shout her name from her number, and she smiles at all of them, because they cannot know how much it helps.
In the last kilometre she thinks about the day she carried a cardboard box onto a bus. That woman could not have imagined this morning, and the thought gives her legs a little more strength.

At the end of the long park path she sees the finishing arch glowing in the sunshine, with a crowd roaring on both sides. She lifts her knees, breathes in and out, and runs towards it as fast as she possibly can.
Dara crosses the finish line with her arms in the air, and tears and laughter come out of her together. Her time is about an hour and twenty minutes, which is not fast, but she has done it.
A volunteer in a bright jacket puts a medal around her neck and wraps a silver blanket around her shoulders. Dara thanks her and walks a few steps before her legs decide that they have had enough.

She sits down on the kerb in the sunshine with her medal and her blanket, and she thinks about the year. The race has shown her that she is stronger than she believed, though strength does not mean that nothing ever hurts.
Hugo finds her first, with Pepper, and then Leila arrives with Samir and Nadia running ahead. Everybody hugs her at once, and Nadia asks to hold the medal, and Dara lets her.
They walk to a small café near the park and eat a huge breakfast of pancakes and bacon. The medal passes from hand to hand around the table, and nobody can stop talking.

That night, after a long bath and a short nap, Dara stands at the fridge and adds a new line to her list. It says, I finished the Riverside Ten, and she hangs the medal on the fridge handle beside it.
A few days after the race Dara sits at the kitchen table with her medal beside her, and she feels flat. She cannot say why, because she has just done the hardest thing of her year.

She tells Hugo on the park bench that she is afraid the old emptiness is coming back. He says that low feelings after a big goal are common, because the climb is over and the mind has no mountain yet.
Dara decides to use her tools, one by one. She breathes slowly, writes the word flat on a page and goes for a short walk by the river.

On Friday Ms Barrow asks her to stay behind and says that the company would like her to take a permanent job. The pay is fair and the work is better than before, and Dara says yes with a smile she cannot hide.

One evening Dara reads a leaflet about a course in managing projects, which meets on Tuesday evenings at the college. She has never been to a class since school, so she fills in the form before she can change her mind.

A month later Dara oversleeps after a bad night, misses her morning run and snaps at Kofi over a small mistake. By lunchtime she feels ashamed, and the old voice says that she has not really changed at all.
She stops and breathes, and she reminds herself that one bad day is not a bad life. Then she buys Kofi a coffee, says she is sorry and finds that he has already forgotten the whole thing.

Dara starts a short review on Sunday evenings, with a mug of tea, a lamp and her notebook. She asks what went well, what was hard and what small thing she will do next week, and it takes only ten minutes.

One Sunday Leila rings to say that she is exhausted by work and the children, and Dara goes straight round. She makes the tea, listens without trying to fix anything and thinks of all the times Leila listened to her.

In the autumn Hugo says he needs an operation on his knee and that he will be resting for several weeks. Dara tells him at once that she will walk Pepper every morning, and for once it is she who knocks on his door.

One evening in September Dara comes home and finds a young man sitting on the stairs with his head in his hands. He is Ben, nineteen, the new neighbour from flat three, and he looks as though he has not slept for days.

She does not tell him to cheer up or ask a string of questions, but sits down two steps below him and waits. After a while he says quietly that it has been a rough month, and she says that she has time to listen.

Ben tells her that he has left his college course and that his parents do not know. He feels like a complete failure, and Dara recognises the empty feeling at once, because she carried it out of an office in a box.

She tells him that feelings cannot be hurried, and that one bad chapter does not make a bad book. Then she offers him a mug of tea and invites him for a walk with Pepper the next morning, and he says maybe.

To her surprise, Ben knocks on her door at seven, and the three of them walk slowly through Linden Park. When she mentions her rule of one small hard thing, he takes out his phone and writes a short email to his tutor.

A few weeks later Dara notices that Ben looks worse, thin and grey, and that his plate is always full when she sees it. He tells her flatly that there is no point in any of it, and the words make her stomach tighten.

She sits across from him in his flat and asks, as gently and calmly as she can, whether he sometimes thinks about ending his life. She has read that asking directly does not make things worse, and Ben says quietly that sometimes he does.

Dara does not panic, and she tells him that she is glad he said so and that he deserves help from someone trained. She stays beside him while he phones his doctor's surgery, and she keeps the number of a crisis line in her own phone.

Hugo, who walks again with a stick, tells them about a terrible rescue that left him unable to sleep for months. A counsellor helped him, and he says that asking for help was the wisest thing he ever did.

That evening Dara sits with Leila in a quiet room and says that she has had heavy nights of her own this year. Leila holds her hand, and Dara decides to book a counsellor, not because she is in danger but because she wants the support.

In her first session Ms Hale listens carefully and asks a few quiet questions, and she never tells Dara what she should feel. Dara learns that counselling is a skilled kind of conversation, and that it is for ordinary people with ordinary heavy days.
A month later Ben has started a different course, and he has an appointment with a doctor each week. He still has hard days, but now he has people and a plan to turn to.

In March, a year after the day she lost her job, Dara opens the cupboard in the hall and finds the old cardboard box. It is a little dusty, and she smiles at it like an old friend who was with her through the hardest part.

She decides that the box should have a new job, and she fills it with her notebooks, her list from the fridge and her medal. It no longer holds what she lost, and it now holds the proof of everything that she has done since.

On a still evening Dara walks along Alder Road with Hugo and Pepper, and Hugo, whose knee is better, asks what has really changed. She thinks about it for a long time and says that she still hurts sometimes, but she no longer faces it alone.

On Sunday she cooks a big dinner in her small flat for Leila, the children, Hugo, Mina, Ben and Ines. They squeeze around a long table, and Dara thanks every one of them, and the noise of their laughing fills the whole building.

Early the next Saturday Dara climbs the long hill in Linden Park with Pepper at her side, before anyone else is awake. At the top she stops to catch her breath and looks out over the grey roofs of the city as the first light touches them.
She sits down on the bench at the top, takes out her notebook and begins to write what she has learned, in plain words. She writes it for herself, and she hopes that one day it will help Ben as well.
Her lessons are short: feel what you feel, speak kindly, breathe slowly, take a small step and ask for help. She adds that rest is part of the plan, and that nobody has to climb alone.
You are stronger than you think, and that strength grows when you use it. Feel what you feel, take one small step, ask for help, and keep going.
C1C2: When Marlow Shoes finally closed its doors, Dara carried six years of her working life out into the afternoon in a single cardboard box. She was twenty-nine, with a small flat and a rent that cared nothing for her feelings, and she felt as though the floor had been quietly removed from beneath her. Nobody had warned her how silent the pavement would seem after the clatter of an office that was never quiet.

On the bus home she sat with the box balanced on her knees and watched the rain trace crooked lines down the glass. People around her scrolled through their phones, argued about dinner and laughed at jokes she could not hear, and none of them knew that her whole map had just been folded away. She waited for a plan to arrive, but all she felt was a vast, ringing emptiness.

In the flat she set the box down on the kitchen floor and could not bring herself to open it, as though unpacking it would make the whole thing official. She sat at the table beside a mug of tea that had gone cold hours earlier, listening to the refrigerator hum. Evening came slowly, grey and unhurried, and found her sitting exactly where she had been at noon, with nothing done.

Later, when the light had faded, the feelings finally caught up with her, and Dara wept on the sofa until her head ached and her breathing was ragged. She did not scold herself or search for a silver lining, because some instinct told her that sorrow pushed down is only sorrow postponed. It was not a pleasant evening, but it was an honest one, and in its quiet way it was the beginning of her recovery.

Her phone began to glow with messages from former colleagues, most of them brisk and hopeful, promising that something better was bound to turn up. Dara read every one of them with a lump in her throat, grateful for the kindness and unable to match the cheerfulness. She set the phone face down and decided that an honest reply could wait until she had one.

For three days Dara slept badly, ate almost nothing and allowed herself to feel whatever came, whether it was fear, anger or plain grief for a life that had ended. A neighbour on the stairs advised her to look on the bright side, but she suspected that sadness hurried away would only return later with interest. Real strength, she was beginning to understand, does not start with pretending that nothing hurts.

On the third night her sister Leila rang, and Dara, almost without thinking, said that she was fine and that there was nothing to worry about. Leila let the silence stretch out for a moment and then said gently that she had known Dara for twenty-nine years and that she did not sound fine at all. Dara held the phone against her ear and found, to her surprise, that she was too tired to argue.

On the fourth morning Dara woke long before dawn and noticed a thought circling in her mind like a bird that could not find a branch: she was a failure, and she always would be. It spoke in such a calm, certain voice that she very nearly accepted it as the truth. Lying there in the dark, she did not yet know that she had a choice about whether to believe it.

At the window she watched the commuters hurry past beneath their umbrellas, each of them carrying some private worry she would never see. A thought, however loud and however often repeated, is not the same as a fact, and it was perfectly possible to hear it without agreeing with it. One bad chapter, however painful to read, does not make the whole book a bad one.

Dara pushed the window wide open and let the cold, clean morning pour into a room that had been stale with sorrow for days. She made a pot of strong tea, found a pen and a notepad, and took the first deliberate step of her new life, which was simply to take stock. Before anything else could be built, she needed to know honestly what was still standing.

Dara sat at the kitchen table and wrote down, in her neatest handwriting, everything she still had. The list proved longer than she had expected, because it held her health, her flat, her sister Leila and a head full of useful knowledge, none of which had been in the box. It was not a cure for anything, but it was a start, and it was written in her own hand.

Then, with her stomach turning slowly over, she opened her bank account and counted her savings with a calculator, to the last pound. There was enough to last about four months, which was neither a comfort nor a catastrophe, merely a fact she could now work with. A number that you can see is almost always less frightening than the fog it replaces.

On a fresh page she set down what six years of customer orders had taught her, and as the list grew she found herself almost embarrassed by it. She was patient, she was quick with figures, and she could soothe a furious stranger on the telephone without ever raising her voice, and none of these gifts had been shut down with the company. Skills, unlike desks and company cars, always go home with the person who owns them, whatever happens to the building.

Waiting for the kettle, Dara thought about the strong people she had known, and it occurred to her that not one of them had simply been handed their strength. Resilience is built the way a muscle is built, through repeated use, a little strain and plenty of recovery, and it is never delivered all at once. If that was true, then her own strength was not missing at all, but merely unexercised after a long season of rest and worry.

At last she knelt beside the cardboard box and unpacked it, placing her mug on the shelf, her photograph beside the bed and the plant on the windowsill.
