The plant was drooping dreadfully, its leaves curled like tired hands, so she gave it a long, slow drink and promised it better days. It was a small gesture of care, and she noticed that it felt oddly like taking care of herself.

On the sixth day a man in a green coat paused at her gate, holding the lead of an elderly spaniel who seemed in no hurry to go anywhere. This was Hugo, the retired firefighter from the house next door, a broad and weathered man in his late sixties with a gentle voice. He had noticed, he said, that her curtains had remained closed for the best part of a week.

Dara stood in the doorway in her dressing gown, aware of her uncombed hair, and said that she really did not feel like going for a walk. Hugo did not argue, lecture or look disappointed, but merely nodded as though she had told him the time. He would knock again tomorrow at seven, he said, and she was perfectly free to say no again.

He sat down on her front step, accepted a mug of tea and explained the single rule he had lived by since the day he left the fire service. Each day, he said, do one small thing that you would rather not do, and do it quickly, before the clever part of your mind can invent an excuse. The point was not to be heroic, he added, but simply to keep proving to yourself that you can still move.

For the rest of the afternoon Dara turned the idea over, searching for a small hard thing of her own that she could manage. In the end she chose to reply to Mina's message, and after four clumsy attempts she wrote that she was frightened but was getting through one day at a time. She pressed send before she could change her mind, and her heart beat as though she had run for a train.

At seven the next morning there was a knock, and Dara, to her own astonishment, was dressed and waiting in her coat. They walked for ten slow minutes behind the spaniel, whose name was Pepper, while the street lay grey and hushed and the first birds began their argument in the trees. When she got back to the flat she was tired, cold and strangely lighter, as if she had set down a small suitcase.

Each morning at seven the knock came, and Dara and Hugo set off along Alder Road behind the unhurried, rolling figure of Pepper. Gradually the street became familiar again, with its tabby cat on the garden wall, its smell of baking from the corner bakery and its neighbours drawing back their curtains one by one. She had walked past these houses for years without once really looking at them, and now she could name every gate.

One morning Hugo paused beneath a lamp post, took a small notebook from his pocket and drew a modest circle with a much larger ring around it. The little circle, he explained, was the comfort zone, the place where everything is familiar and nothing can surprise us, and it feels wonderfully safe. The trouble is that it does not stay the same size, because a life lived entirely inside it will quietly shrink.

Back at the flat Dara looked at the heap of unopened letters on the sofa and the silent telephone beside them, and she understood something uncomfortable. Her own circle had been contracting ever since the day she lost her job, and in only a few weeks she had begun to avoid the post, the phone and even the corner shop. Nothing had forced her to withdraw; she had simply, one small retreat at a time, backed away.

That day she chose the obvious hard thing: she opened every letter and telephoned the gas company about a bill that looked suspiciously large. The call lasted six minutes, a cheerful stranger admitted that a meter reading had been wrong, and the mistake was corrected on the spot. Dara put the receiver down feeling a full inch taller, as though she had defeated something far bigger than a bill.

On Saturday Hugo took her to the community pool in Linden Park, where he swam a few slow lengths every week whatever the weather. Dara stood at the edge in her old swimming costume, gazing down at the pale blue water and the faint, shivering tiles beneath it, and her feet refused to move. Every sensible part of her mind explained that it would be freezing and that nobody could possibly expect her to enter.

Hugo said nothing for a while, then pointed to the lifeguard, to the notice on the wall and finally to the water, and asked her a question. Was this truly dangerous, he wondered aloud, or was it merely uncomfortable, which is a quite different thing? Over thirty years he had learned that the two are easy to confuse, and that most of what we avoid belongs firmly to the second kind.

Dara sat on the edge, slid down into the water and gasped as the cold seized her chest and drove the breath from her lungs. She flapped her arms, spluttered and then began to laugh, helplessly and loudly, as the feeling of danger slowly dissolved into something closer to delight. Nothing terrible had happened; she was simply wet, cold and, for the first time in weeks, entirely awake.

Later that week she had to telephone a company about a possible job, and as she dialled her heart began to hammer and her palms turned damp. Hugo had told her that fear and excitement feel remarkably alike in the body, with the same quickened pulse, the same fluttering stomach and the same restless hands. The body, it seemed, sounds one alarm for two very different feelings and leaves the mind to decide which is which.

He had suggested that she try telling herself, I am excited, rather than I am scared, before she spoke. Dara felt faintly ridiculous whispering it to an empty kitchen, but she did it anyway, and when the line connected her voice emerged steadier than she had dared hope. It was not magic, and Hugo never claimed that it was; it was simply a way of choosing which story to tell about the same racing heart.

On the kitchen wall Dara had pinned a large calendar, and every evening she drew a blue cross through the day if she had kept her promise to do one small hard thing. After two weeks the crosses formed an unbroken chain of fourteen, and she was startled by how fiercely she wanted to protect it. A streak, she was discovering, is a quiet kind of proof that you are the sort of person who keeps showing up.

At three o'clock one morning Dara woke with her heart thudding against her ribs and a long, tangled list of worries unspooling in her mind. She turned over, checked the clock twice and knew with the weary certainty of the sleepless that the night would not now return to her. Outside, the street lamp hummed, and the world seemed to be made entirely of problems.

On their next walk she confessed the sleepless night to Hugo, and he stopped on the pavement, held up his hand and began to demonstrate. Breathe in through your nose for a count of four, he said, ticking the numbers off on his fingers, and then out through your mouth for a count of six. His voice had the calm, unhurried quality of a man who had spent decades speaking to people on the worst night of their lives.

A breath out that is longer than the breath in, he explained, tends to slow the heart and ease the body towards calm, though it is no cure for anything and it will not solve a single real problem. Dara practised in her armchair every afternoon with her eyes closed and her hands loose in her lap, feeling faintly foolish at first. After a few days she began to notice that the tightness in her chest loosened a little sooner each time.

One morning, as her stomach knotted before an important telephone call, she took a pen and wrote the single word nervous on the corner of a page. Hugo had told her that giving a feeling its proper name can reduce its force, and she was sceptical, as she was sceptical of most simple remedies. To her surprise, the word on the paper seemed to shrink the feeling inside her until she could look at it calmly.

She began to keep a running list of what she felt each day, and it was an odd and honest collection: ashamed, hopeful, furious, bored and then ashamed all over again. Hugo told her that feelings behave like waves, swelling to a peak and falling away, and that even the ones that seem endless are usually passing through. It was strangely comforting to think of her sorrow as weather rather than as a permanent climate.

One evening Dara caught sight of herself in the hall mirror, and for a moment she listened properly to what she had been saying inside her head. Stupid, useless, hopeless, ran the familiar chorus, and she realised with a jolt that she would never have spoken to a friend in that tone. She had been her own harshest critic for so long that she had mistaken the cruelty for honesty.

So she tried an experiment, standing in front of the mirror and addressing her reflection in the voice she would use for her sister Leila on a bad day. It felt peculiar, and her cheeks grew hot as though someone might overhear, but the sharpest edge of the thought did soften a little. Kindness, she noted, was not the same as flattery, and she could be gentle with herself without lying.

On another night the worries would not stop circling, so Dara took a sheet of paper and wrote every single one of them down in a fast, untidy scrawl. She folded the page twice, tucked it into the kitchen drawer and closed the drawer with a small, deliberate bang, as if sealing a door. Her head, once emptied onto the paper, felt lighter and considerably less crowded, and for the first time in a week she slept.

Within days she had turned the habit into a rule: ten minutes of worry time at six every evening, with a kitchen timer and a notebook. If a worry came knocking at any other hour, she told it politely that it would have to wait until six, and rather to her amazement most of them did. When the timer rang she shut the notebook, and the worrying, for that day at least, was finished.

A week later she took out the old page of worries and read it through with a pen in her hand, crossing out the ones that had come to nothing. Nearly all of them had never happened, and the few that had were smaller and more manageable than they had seemed at three in the morning. This does not mean that every fear is groundless, she reminded herself, but the mind is a poor forecaster when it is frightened and tired.

Armed with Hugo's old pen and her own stubborn good sense, Dara updated her CV and sent out twelve applications in the space of a single week. Each time she pressed the button she felt a small flutter of hope, like releasing a paper boat onto a fast stream, and then she closed the laptop and went out for a walk. It was a clever way of keeping herself from staring at the screen and refreshing the inbox every thirty seconds.

The first reply arrived on Thursday morning, a courteous email that began with the words thank you for your interest and ended, inevitably, with the word unfortunately. Dara read it three times, and each reading landed like a small, polite punch somewhere beneath her ribs. She had expected to feel disappointed, but she had not expected it to feel so personal.

She gave herself exactly one hour to be miserable, with a pot of tea and no apologies, and then she took a pen and a clean sheet of paper. Instead of demanding what was wrong with her, she asked a quieter and more useful question: what could she do better next time? A rejection, she decided, is a piece of information about one particular fit, and not a verdict on her whole character.

Over the next fortnight three more refusals trickled in, while the great majority of the companies simply never replied at all. Hugo, who had applied for a few jobs in his own time, assured her that this was entirely normal and that a long silence usually tells you more about a busy office than about the person who applied. Dara nodded, but she still checked her inbox far more often than was healthy.

Summoning her courage, she wrote to one of the firms and asked, as politely as she could, whether they would be willing to tell her why she had not been chosen. To her astonishment a real person replied within two days, in a message that was brief, kind and unexpectedly generous. It contained just one piece of advice, but that advice was worth more to her than a dozen cheerful messages.

Her CV, the stranger observed, listed everything she had been responsible for but never once said what she had actually achieved. Dara rewrote it that evening, replacing vague claims with concrete figures: she had cut errors in customer orders by about a third, and she had handled around forty calls every day. The same six years suddenly looked like the record of someone who got things done.

On Sunday evening Hugo put on his reading glasses, produced a clipboard and took the part of the interviewer at his kitchen table with magnificent seriousness. His first question was the oldest and the most dreaded, tell me about yourself, and Dara's mind went as white and blank as the page in front of him. She opened her mouth to answer, and nothing at all came out except a small, embarrassed squeak.

She floundered through an answer, apologised twice and began to laugh, and Hugo, far from being discouraged, told her gently to start again from the beginning. By the fourth attempt she had found a short, honest story about her six years at Marlow Shoes, and the words flowed with a naturalness that astonished them both. Practice, she realised, does not remove the nerves, but it gives them somewhere sensible to go.

A week later Halden Logistics invited her to an interview, and she arrived twenty minutes early in her best shirt with her notes on her knee. In the bright, humming lobby she breathed out slowly for a count of six and told herself, with only a faint sense of absurdity, that she was excited. Her palms were damp, but her thoughts were clear, and she was, against every expectation, quite ready to begin.

The interview went well, apart from one question about a computer system that she had never used in her life. She might have bluffed, but instead she said plainly that she did not know the system, that she learned new ones quickly and that she would be glad to show them how. The two interviewers exchanged a glance that she could not interpret, and she walked out into the sunshine with her head held high.

The email from Halden Logistics arrived on Monday morning, brief and kindly worded, saying that they had chosen a candidate with more experience. They added, with what she suspected was genuine warmth, that she had been a very close second, and that she should apply again. Dara thanked them, closed the laptop and felt her shoulders slowly sink, as if the news had been resting on them.

A few days later, halfway through their usual walk, Dara sat down heavily on a bench in Linden Park and discovered that she could not go on. It was a tiredness that sleep did not seem to touch, a heaviness in her arms and legs that made the whole morning feel like wading through wet sand. She wondered, with a flicker of real alarm, whether she had anything left at all.

Hugo did not hurry her, hold out his hand or deliver a speech, but sat beside her in the pale sunshine until her breathing had settled. Tired, he said at last, does not always mean empty, and the two are easier to mistake than people think. They climbed the gentle hill a little further together at a very slow pace, and he reminded her to listen for real pain, which is a different thing from ordinary effort.

That night Dara took an honest look at how she had been living, and she resolved to build on three plain foundations, beginning with sleep. She chose a sensible bedtime, switched off the lamp at the proper hour and left her phone charging in the kitchen, where its glowing screen could not tempt her. It was hardly a dramatic reform, but sleep, she was learning, is the quiet floor on which everything else stands.

The second foundation was food, and she stopped skipping lunch and letting biscuits stand in for dinner, which had been her habit since the day of the box. She cooked simple, plentiful meals of beans, rice and vegetables, nothing fashionable or expensive, and she noticed that her afternoons grew steadier and her temper a good deal sweeter. Nobody had told her that a bowl of soup could be a form of courage.

The third foundation was movement, and Dara placed her old trainers beside the front door, where she could not possibly overlook them on her way out. Hugo had told her that it is much easier to begin when the next step is already waiting in front of you, and she was inclined to believe him. The shoes sat there each night like a patient dog, asking for nothing and reminding her of everything.

Each morning, before she let herself do anything else, Dara made her bed, pulling the sheets tight and squaring the corners with a precision that would have pleased a sergeant. It took less than a minute, but it gave her a quiet sense of order and a first small victory before the day had even begun. A made bed, she found, is a tiny argument against chaos, and it is one that she could win before breakfast every single day.

She wrote a short morning routine on an index card and stuck it to the bathroom mirror: a glass of water, the bed, the trainers and one hard thing. It was not a clever system, and nobody would ever publish it in a book, but it spared her from having to make every decision while she was still half asleep. Routine, she discovered, is what remains to carry you through the hours when willpower is not yet awake.

After a particularly bad night Dara woke feeling heavy and cross, and every part of her wanted to disappear back under the blankets and stay there. Instead she carried out the smallest possible version of her routine, a glass of water and a made bed, and then sat on the edge of the mattress feeling faintly victorious. A tiny effort on a terrible day, she told herself, is worth far more than a magnificent effort that never takes place.

On the way home from the park Dara paused at the gate, where a bright poster had been tied with string to the railings, flapping in the wind. It announced the Riverside Ten, a charity run of ten kilometres to raise money for the local food bank, to be held in exactly twelve weeks. She smiled, shook her head at the sheer absurdity of the idea and walked on, but the poster stayed in her mind like a pebble in a shoe.

Dara laughed out loud at the poster, for she could not even run for a bus without losing her breath and her dignity in the same moment. Behind her, as if on cue, a number nine bus pulled away from the stop and trundled off up the road without her. It seemed to prove the point so neatly that she half expected the idea to die there on the pavement.

That evening she mentioned the poster to Hugo in the tone of someone telling a joke, and he did not push her in either direction. He asked only what would make it a good yes for her, and then he waited, as he always did, with the patience of a man who had learned not to rush other people's answers. The question sat between them in the dusk for a long time, and neither of them hurried to fill the silence.

At the kitchen table Dara wrote three reasons in her notebook, and she was surprised to find how quickly the honest ones came. She did not wish to impress anyone, since the people who mattered would love her whether she finished or not, but she wanted to prove something to herself, and the money raised would feed real families. It was a modest list, and it was enough to set her pen moving.

On Saturday she walked into Stride Sports and signed the entry form at the counter before her courage had time to leave by the back door. Jo, a cheerful assistant with a tape measure around her neck, watched her walk up and down the shop and then chose a pair of running shoes that fitted her feet properly. Dara handed over her card with a mixture of terror and joy, because the shoes were an act of belief that she could not take back.

That evening Dara telephoned her sister Leila, half expecting to be laughed at, and the response was a shriek so piercing that she had to hold the phone at arm's length. Leila declared that she would be there at the finish line with a banner, two excited children and an alarming quantity of snacks. Dara put the phone down smiling, aware that she now had an audience that she could not disappoint.

Hugo helped her draw up a gradual plan in which short bursts of running were mixed with plenty of walking, and every few days there was a full day of rest. They pinned it to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a pear, and Dara was amazed at how small and unthreatening the first week looked. A mountain, it seemed, could be made from pieces small enough to carry in one hand.

Hugo explained that most beginners are hurt not by doing too little but by doing too much too soon, when the enthusiasm of the heart outruns the readiness of the legs. The plan was slow on purpose, he said, and a rest day was not laziness but the time when the body quietly gets stronger. She wrote that sentence on the corner of the plan, because she suspected that she would need to read it again.

On Monday morning Dara ran for two whole minutes along the park path in her stiff new shoes, her arms flapping and her face turning the colour of a ripe tomato. She stopped, bent double and laughed between gasps, because it was the longest she had run since she was sixteen and the sky had not fallen. Two minutes, she thought, is not very long, but it is also infinitely longer than none.

The next morning her legs were so sore that she went down the stairs sideways, clutching the banister with both hands like an elderly sailor on a rolling deck. Hugo told her that such stiffness is common after anything new and usually fades within a few days, and she was grateful that the plan declared this a day of rest. She spent it stretching gently and feeling smug, which was not what she had expected from a rest day.

By Sunday Dara had completed the first week of the plan, and she drew a neat blue tick beside it on the fridge with unnecessary ceremony. She sent a message to Mina describing the whole adventure, and the reply came back at once, a long row of cheering faces followed by a demand for photographs. It was the first time since March that someone had celebrated something she had done.

On Thursday the rain beat so hard against the window that the glass seemed to tremble, and the plan on the fridge declared it a run day. Dara pulled the blankets up over her head and informed the ceiling that nobody on earth would blame her for staying exactly where she was. It was a very persuasive argument, and she could feel herself being convinced by it.

Instead she put on her yellow jacket, pulled the hood tight around her face and made a bargain with herself to do less rather than nothing. She walked for ten dripping minutes through the empty streets, splashing through puddles, and when she got home she felt as proud as if she had finished a marathon. The lesson she took from that morning was a simple one: on the hardest days, showing up small beats not showing up at all.

Hugo told her that people keep their promises far more often when they plan for the difficult moments before those moments arrive, and he called the method an if-then plan. If it rains, then I wear the yellow jacket and go out for ten minutes, he suggested, in the cheerful tone of a man reading a recipe. The beauty of it, he said, is that the decision has been made by your calmer self, long before your tired self gets a vote.

That evening Dara wrote out cards for her four favourite excuses, which were tired, cold, busy and embarrassed, and she pinned them in a neat row to the fridge. Every card began with the word if and ended with a modest, sensible action that she could genuinely carry out, such as lacing her shoes and stepping outside for just five minutes. She felt rather like a general preparing for a long campaign against herself, with the cards as her only soldiers.

On Saturday a tall, long-legged runner overtook her on the path with effortless grace, and Dara kept her eyes fixed on her feet, absolutely certain that the whole park was staring at her. Hugo, when she described it later, remarked that most people are far too busy thinking about themselves to notice a red-faced beginner puffing along behind them. The audience she imagined, he said, was almost entirely in her own head, and it was a very unforgiving one.

Further along the river path a smiling woman in a bright cap waved and slowed her pace to jog beside Dara for a moment, humming cheerfully as she went. Her name was Ines, she was somewhere in her sixties, and she declared without a trace of embarrassment that she was no faster than a determined snail. We are all beginners, she added, and every single runner on this path remembers the first morning when they thought they would never make it to the end of the road.

In the third week the plan asked her to run for five whole minutes without stopping, a distance that had seemed utterly out of reach only a month before. She counted her breaths, kept her shoulders loose and fixed her eyes on a distant lamp post, and when the watch finally beeped she realised with astonishment that she could have gone on a little longer. It was a strange and delightful discovery to learn that the limit she had feared was not where she had thought it was.

On a still, bright morning she reached the river path just as the sun lifted above the trees and set the whole surface of the water on fire. For the first time she was not counting the seconds or willing the run to be over, for she was simply moving in a steady rhythm, enjoying the cool air and the soft thud of her own feet. It was a small moment, but she knew at once that it would stay with her.

One day she noticed that she had climbed the stairs of her building two at a time without even thinking about it, and she stopped on the landing and laughed. She was sleeping more deeply, her moods were steadier, and her shoulders no longer lived up near her ears, and all of these changes had arrived so quietly that she had nearly missed them. Progress, she was learning, rarely announces itself; it simply accumulates, one unremarkable morning after another.

At the end of the fourth week Dara sat down with a calculator and her bank statement and finally did the sum that she had been avoiding for days. She had about six weeks of savings left, and the old fear, which she had thought was fading, came rushing back into her stomach like cold water. She did not pretend that it was not there; she set down her pen, breathed out slowly for a count of six and let herself feel it.

On Sunday Dara took the bus to her sister's house, where her nephew and niece, Samir and Nadia, hurled themselves at her legs the moment the door opened. She smiled brightly, handed over the biscuits she had brought and told the whole family that she was doing wonderfully, thank you, and that the job hunt was going very well. It was the sort of performance that she could have given in her sleep.

After lunch Leila found her alone in the kitchen with a cup of tea going cold, and without saying a word she sat down at the table opposite her. This time Dara did not say that she was fine; her voice cracked, and she admitted that she was terrified about money and that some days she felt completely useless. Saying it aloud was like opening a window in a room where the air had been stale for months.

Leila did not try to fix everything or promise that it would all work out in the end, but simply listened, with one hand resting on her sister's arm. Only when Dara had finished did she offer practical help, saying that she would gladly read through the CV and cook an extra dinner every Sunday, and Dara accepted both with a lump in her throat. Being listened to, she discovered, can be more useful than any amount of advice.

Watching Leila rock a sleepy Nadia against her shoulder, Dara thought how readily she herself would help her sister at any hour of the day or night, and how little it would change her opinion of Leila. If that was true, then perhaps asking for help was not weakness at all, but a perfectly ordinary part of being a person among other people. The idea seemed so obvious that she was embarrassed it had taken her twenty-nine years to find it.

On Friday Mina and Tomas came to dinner, bringing a bottle of lemonade and some very bad jokes, and the three of them laughed until the plates were stone cold. Dara noticed that she felt stronger after an evening spent among people who were openly glad to see her, and she resolved not to let the old habit of hiding return. Supportive company, she thought, works a little like a good pair of shoes, because you only notice its value over a long distance.

Another friend, Gareth, spent the whole of a coffee complaining about his boss, his neighbours and the weather, and Dara went home feeling as though someone had pulled a plug out of her energy. She could not choose every person in her life, but she could decide how much time she gave to each, and she told him kindly that she needed a different kind of conversation. To her relief, he did not take offence; he looked rather as though he had been waiting for someone to say it.

While helping Leila clear out the attic one wet afternoon, Dara found a battered exam paper at the bottom of a cardboard box, with a large red mark slashed across the top. It was the maths exam she had failed at sixteen, and she remembered, as if it had happened that morning, crying in the school toilets and deciding that she was simply a person who could not do numbers. The memory had been quietly guiding her choices for thirteen years, and she had never once stopped to question it.

She sat down on an old trunk and read through her notes with the cool curiosity of a stranger, and she saw at once what the girl of sixteen had not been able to see. She had never asked her teacher for help, not once, and when she finally did, the following term, she had passed at the second attempt with a perfectly respectable mark. The paper was not evidence of a flaw in her; it was a lesson that she had learned and then, somehow, forgotten.

At the library Dara borrowed a book about how people cope with hard times, and she read, with surprise, that most people recover far better than they expect to. The author was careful to add that some people need more support, that recovery is rarely a straight line and that reaching out to a professional is a sign of good sense and not of failure. Dara copied that sentence into her notebook and underlined it twice, because she suspected that she would need it again.

One morning she ran all the way to the river, stopped on the bridge with her hands on her knees and watched the sun rise slowly over the water. She was out of breath, her shoes were soaked and her hair was a disgrace, and yet for the first time in months she felt something small and steady stirring inside her. It was hope, she realised, not the loud and glittering kind, but the quiet sort that simply gets up each morning and goes to work.

Every night before bed Dara wrote three good things from the day in a small notebook with a blue cover. On the first night she stared at the blank page for ten whole minutes, and in the end she could produce only a slice of toast, a dry pavement and a short, kind text from Mina. It was hardly a triumph, but she wrote them down with great ceremony and drew a tiny star beside each one.

Hugo had told her that the point of the exercise was not to be falsely cheerful but to train the mind to notice what is already there, as one trains a muscle. The effect, he admitted, is modest, and not everyone feels it, but it costs nothing and takes two minutes. Dara decided that she could afford to try an experiment that cheap, and that the worst outcome was two quiet minutes.

Over the following weeks she began to notice small things as she moved through her days, almost against her will. A café worker remembered her name and her order, a sparrow hopped boldly onto her table to steal a crumb, and Pepper's tail wagged each morning as though she were a film star arriving at a premiere. The world around her had not changed in the least, but the way that she attended to it had changed completely.

On other pages she wrote down the hard things too, because she had no wish to pretend that the bad days had vanished or to scold herself for having them. Good things do not cancel out the hard ones, she understood, and nobody should be made to feel that they must be grateful for their troubles. What the notebook did was remind her that a difficult day is only one chapter, and never the whole book.

In the fifth week the plan asked her for eight minutes of running, and she did it in the park under the new green leaves, her arms swinging easily at her sides. When the watch beeped she was breathing hard but smiling broadly, and for the first time the idea of finishing the whole race did not feel like a joke. She was stronger than she had been, and her body was beginning to say so.

In the sixth week, feeling suddenly invincible, Dara ran too fast down the long hill in the park, and the toe of her shoe caught the edge of a kerb. She felt something twist sharply in her ankle and sat down hard on the pavement, her eyes filling with tears of pain and sheer surprise. Her first thought, strangely, was not of the pain but of the poster on the park gate.

Hugo, who had been strolling a little way behind with Pepper, hurried over, helped her to her feet and half carried her home along Alder Road, saying very little. He settled her on the sofa with her foot raised on a cushion and held a bag of frozen peas against the swelling, with the practised calm of a man who had seen a great many ankles. Dara was grateful and mortified in exactly equal measure, and she could not decide which feeling to apologise for first.

When he had gone, Dara picked up one of her trainers and hurled it across the room, where it bounced off the wall and landed, with a hollow thump, in the laundry basket. She was furious, not with the kerb or the hill but with herself, because six weeks of effort seemed to be draining away through a swollen ankle. Anger, she noticed, was a feeling, and for once she let it burn itself out.

That night she lay awake with her foot propped on a tower of pillows, quite certain that the race was over and that she had failed at the one thing she had dared to try. The old voice in her head was back, speaking in its calm, reasonable tone, saying that she should never have believed she could do it. She did not have the strength to argue with it, so she simply listened and waited for the dawn.

The next morning Hugo came to her table with two mugs of tea and sat down heavily opposite her without any announcement. A setback, he told her, is a bend in the road and not the end of it, and the first thing to do on a bend is to slow down and see what is round the corner. Dara picked up the telephone, rang the surgery and booked an appointment for that afternoon.

Dr Anand turned Dara's ankle gently from side to side, pressed a few tender places and asked her to walk slowly across the consulting room. It was a mild sprain, she said, and the best medicine now was rest, followed by a gradual return to activity, with a physiotherapist to help if the ankle did not improve. She spoke without drama, which was reassuring, and she did not once promise that the race was lost.

On the clinic steps Dara read the leaflet, which advised about ten days of rest before she attempted any running, and her heart sank into her shoes. Resting felt like a kind of failure, and she could not stop imagining everyone else surging ahead, training harder and growing stronger while she sat on a sofa with her foot in the air. It is remarkable how loudly the mind can insist that standing still means falling behind.

That evening Hugo lifted the leg of his trousers on her doorstep and showed her a long, pale scar that curved around his knee like a river on a map. Years ago, he said, he had run on an injury because he was too proud to stop, had turned a small problem into a large one and had lost an entire season. Knowing when to rest, he told her, is a part of strength and not its opposite.

Dara decided that resting need not mean doing nothing at all, so she went to the community pool, where swimming put no weight on her ankle. She swam slow, steady lengths, feeling the water hold her up, and she was glad to discover that her fitness had not simply evaporated. If one road is closed for repairs, she thought, there is no law against taking another to the same village.

One afternoon she floated on her back in the middle of the pool, gazing up at the long white lights on the ceiling and listening to the muffled echoes of splashing. She remembered how terrified she had been of this very water on the first morning, standing on the edge in her old swimming costume, and she smiled at how far away that woman seemed. The cold that had once felt like an enemy now felt like a friend.

At home she performed the gentle exercises that Dr Anand had demonstrated, such as tracing the letters of the alphabet in the air with her toes while she sat on a chair. It was boring, a little silly and quite impossible to do while looking dignified, but she did it every day without fail. Healing, she had learned, is often undramatic, and it rewards those who do the dull things faithfully.

One night, when the flat was silent and the plan on the fridge seemed like a joke told by a stranger, doubt returned in force. Dara put her hands over her face and whispered that she could not do this, that she had never been able to do anything of the kind, and for a few minutes she believed it entirely. Doubt is a visitor that always seems to arrive when the lights are low and no one else is awake.

Then she remembered something Hugo had said about the words we choose to use, and she took out an index card and a pen. She crossed out the words I can't and wrote in their place, in firm capital letters, I CAN DO THE NEXT STEP, and she stuck the card on the wall above her bed. It did not abolish the doubt, but it gave her something true to say back to it.

In the morning she looked only at the single thing in front of her, which was tying her shoelaces on the doorstep in the pale, early light. She had learned that nobody climbs a whole mountain in one stride, and that when you gaze at the summit the climb looks impossible, whereas the next step on the path is always small enough to manage. So she tied the laces, double knots on both feet, and stood up with the quiet satisfaction of someone who has decided.

Ten days later Dr Anand pronounced the ankle much improved and gave Dara permission to begin again, gently and slowly. Hugo helped her to design a new plan with plenty more walking in it, for the aim of the Riverside Ten was now simply to finish, not to finish fast. She should be proud to cross the line at any speed, he said, and Dara found, to her surprise, that this new goal felt lighter and more honest.

At the end of the month Dara opened her bank account and found that the figure at the bottom had shrunk to almost nothing. The old fear lurched in her stomach, but instead of closing the page, as she once would have done, she made herself look at the number for a full minute. Fear, she was learning, becomes smaller when it is stared at steadily, though it never becomes comfortable company.

Hugo listened to her worries on a bench in Linden Park without once telling her that everything would be fine, which she appreciated more than she could say. A job that is less than you hoped for, he said, can still be a bridge, because a bridge does not have to be beautiful in order to carry you to the other side. He had himself taken a dull job as a security guard for a year, he added, before the next good thing arrived.

On Friday afternoon a recruitment agency telephoned with an offer of three months of temporary work in the office of Brightwell Supplies. The tasks sounded duller than anything she had done at Marlow Shoes, and the pay was noticeably lower, and she felt her pride rise up like a wall between herself and the telephone. Behind that wall, however, she could hear the quiet, relentless arithmetic of her rent and her food and her bills.

She slept on the offer, and in the morning she wrote the advantages and the disadvantages in two columns on a sheet of paper and discovered that the good column was the longer one. She rang the agency back and said yes, and when she shook hands that afternoon with her new manager, Ms Barrow, a brisk, kind woman with half-moon glasses, she found that she was smiling. Pride, it turned out, was much easier to set down than she had imagined.

On her first day at Brightwell the desks were unfamiliar, the computer system was baffling and everyone around her seemed to know precisely what they were doing. Dara had not been a beginner for six years, and the sensation was oddly physical, like wearing a coat that was a size too small and having to pretend that it fitted. She felt clumsy, slow and faintly absurd, and she wanted very much to go home.

But she made up her mind to accept that she was a beginner, since the only way to stop being one is to go through it, and she began to ask questions, one after another, all day. Kofi, a cheerful man at the next desk who wore a different bright tie every morning, answered each one with endless patience and never once made her feel stupid. Learning, she thought, is far less lonely when someone is willing to show you where the buttons are.

On Thursday she sent an order to the wrong address, and her stomach dropped through the floor when she saw her mistake glowing on the screen. She walked straight to Ms Barrow's desk, explained exactly what had happened and proposed a plan to put it right, and the parcel was recovered and redirected within the hour. Owning a mistake quickly, she realised, is oddly freeing, because the dreadful secret has nowhere to grow.

That evening she told Hugo about her error over tea in his kitchen, where an old fire helmet sat on a shelf above the toaster like a retired hero. He laughed warmly and said that every firefighter in the world had once been a rookie who tripped over the hose, and that the whole station remembered it for years afterwards, with affection. Nobody expects a beginner to be perfect, he said, only to be honest and to keep learning.

On Friday an angry customer telephoned about a lost delivery, and Dara answered in the calm, steady voice that she had perfected over six years at Marlow Shoes. She listened without interrupting, repeated the problem back to him, offered a clear solution and ended the call with thanks, and across the room Ms Barrow lowered her glasses and nodded slowly. The skills on her list had come with her after all, and they were still her own.

By the end of the first week Dara was weary but, to her surprise, not unhappy, for the job was less dreadful than she had feared and the people were kind. On Saturday she ran gently along the river at dawn, her ankle holding firm, with a light heart and a feeling that something was beginning to turn. A first pay cheque was due at the end of the month, and the number at the bottom of her account would soon stop shrinking.

On Tuesday Ms Barrow asked Dara, in the offhand way of someone mentioning the weather, whether she would explain her new order checks to the whole team at Friday's meeting. Dara said that of course she could, in a bright voice that belonged to somebody else entirely, and then walked back to her desk feeling distinctly unwell. Her hands were already damp, and the meeting was still three whole days away, which left plenty of time to dread it.

All afternoon she pictured herself standing at the front of the room, twenty pairs of eyes trained on her, her hands shaking visibly, her mouth full of cotton. She longed to go back to Ms Barrow's office and say that she had changed her mind, and the urge was so strong and so reasonable-sounding that it almost frightened her. Avoidance, she saw, always sounds perfectly sensible at the very moment when it is speaking to you.

Instead she told herself that it was possible to say yes and to be afraid at the same moment, since the two did not cancel each other out. That evening she wrote five short points on index cards, one idea per card, and she practised the talk aloud at the kitchen table, over and over, until the words stopped feeling like a foreign language. A fear that has been rehearsed against is a good deal smaller than one that has been left to grow in the dark.

On Wednesday she practised in Hugo's kitchen, with Pepper as her only other audience and Hugo listening with his arms folded and his head on one side. Nerves, he told her, are not a sign that she would fail but a sign that she cared about doing it well, and the very best speakers feel exactly the same flutter before they begin. The difference is that they have learned to carry it with them rather than wait for it to leave.

On Thursday night she lay in bed and breathed in for four counts and out for six until she felt her shoulders drop away from her ears and the knot in her stomach loosen. She also made one if-then plan, which she repeated like a charm: if I lose my place, then I will stop, look at my card and take one slow breath. It was a modest safety net, but a net, she knew, makes the high wire feel a good deal lower.

On Friday she stood at the front of the meeting room with a single card in her hand, and for a long, awful second no sound emerged from her mouth at all. Then she remembered what Hugo had said about starting small, and she began with one sentence only: today I would like to show you three small changes. The sentence hung in the air, steady and ordinary, and she realised that she had survived the hardest part.

Her hands were trembling so violently that the card shook like a leaf in the wind, and she was sure that every person in the room could see it. She noticed this, named it silently as excitement and went on speaking, and to her great surprise her voice came out clear, level and almost calm. It is possible, she discovered, for the body to panic while the voice carries on doing its job.

Halfway through her explanation her mind went entirely blank, and she lost her place, and a heavy silence settled over the room. She did exactly what she had planned, which was to stop, look down at her card, take one slow breath and find the line again, and nobody in the room seemed to mind at all. A pause, which had felt like a cliff edge to her, looked to everyone else like a perfectly ordinary person thinking.

When she spoke her last sentence her colleagues clapped politely, and Ms Barrow gave a small, approving nod from the back of the room. The talk had not been perfect, and it had certainly not been brilliant, but it had been perfectly fine, and she had survived it with her dignity intact. She sat down and noticed, with a small private smile, that her hands were, at last, perfectly still.

At the end of the afternoon Kofi came over holding one of the new address labels and told her that her idea had saved him an hour that very morning. Dara felt a warmth spread across her chest, because the real reward of the whole terrifying exercise was not the applause but the simple discovery that her work had helped someone. She had been so busy fearing the audience that she had forgotten to ask what she might give it.

On Sunday evening Dara sat at the kitchen table with a pen and a clean sheet of paper and wrote down every hard thing she had done since March. The list included the call to the gas company, the first plunge into the cold pool, the interview, the two-minute run and the talk in the meeting room. By the time she had finished it filled the whole page, and it was far longer than she would ever have guessed.

She stuck the list to the fridge with the pear-shaped magnet, and she told herself firmly that it was not there to make her vain but to serve as evidence. Feelings, as she now knew well, can be loud and persuasive and quite wrong, whereas a page of written facts will stay steady on a bad day. A list cannot be talked out of what is true, and it does not care how tired its author happens to feel.

On Tuesday evening she had a thoroughly bad day, with a mistake at work, a long grey mood and the old voice murmuring that she was fooling everybody. She stood in front of the fridge with a mug of tea and read the list from top to bottom, slowly, as though it described somebody else. The person on that page, she thought, did not sound like a failure at all.

She made it a rule to add one new line every week, even for achievements that seemed small enough to be silly, because the small ones are the bricks of the wall. This week she wrote the words I asked Kofi for help, since the old Dara would have hidden the problem and let it grow rather than admit that she did not know. The list was becoming, in its modest way, a portrait of someone she was rather beginning to like.

In the tenth week Dara met Ines on the river path, and the two of them walked and ran six kilometres together at a comfortable chatting pace, the sun warm on their shoulders. Ines told her stories about her own first race, in which she had finished second from last and had been absolutely thrilled about it, and Dara laughed so much that she had to stop and hold her side. Courage, it seemed, travels a great deal better in company, and she wondered why she had tried to carry hers alone for so long.

At Stride Sports Jo helped her choose some soft running socks and a small water bottle that would clip to her belt, and she gave a piece of advice that Dara wrote down at once. Never try anything new on race day, she said, because even a very good new shoe can rub a blister on a long run, and the day of the race is for trusting what you have already tested. It was, Dara thought, excellent advice for a good many things in life, from interviews to friendships to new habits.

On Wednesday her race number arrived in the post, a white square printed in bold black digits, and she pinned it to her running top in front of the bedroom mirror. Her stomach turned over in a way that was impossible to name, since it felt like fear and excitement at the same time, the same flutter and the same racing pulse. She looked at the woman in the mirror and decided, for the moment, to call it excitement.

That night she lay awake worrying that she would come in last, with the other runners long gone, the crowd drifting home and the finishing arch standing empty and silent. She confessed this to Hugo over the garden gate the next morning, and he said, with a kind of gruff tenderness, that last place still means that somebody finished, whereas so many people never find the courage even to start. Dara turned that over all day and found that it weighed more than her worry.

On Sunday morning Dara and Hugo set out along the river, and she walked and ran eight kilometres, the farthest she had ever gone in her life, with Pepper trundling happily behind. Her ankle held up, her breathing stayed calm, and at the end she stood bent over with her hands on her knees, tired in every muscle and grinning like a child. Eight kilometres, she thought, is almost ten, and ten, which had once been a joke on a poster, was starting to feel real.

That evening Leila sent a photograph of Samir and Nadia lying on the floor of the living room, painting a banner in large, wobbling letters of every colour in the paint box. It said GO AUNTIE DARA, with one letter backwards and a purple dragon in the corner for reasons that nobody could explain. Dara looked at the picture for a long time, and her eyes grew hot and blurry, and she was not at all sure that she minded.

At the start of the eleventh week the radio warned of heavy rain and strong winds, and Dara gazed at the plan on the fridge with a sinking heart. She had come all this way, through the ankle and the interview and the speech, and now the weather itself seemed determined to say no. It was the perfect moment, she thought grimly, to test what her if-then cards were worth.

Her card said that if the weather turned dangerous she would train indoors, so she spent twenty minutes stepping up and down the stairs of her building, past the cold radiators and the potted palm. She felt ridiculous for the first five minutes and rather wonderful for the rest, and the neighbour on the landing, a retired man with a newspaper, gave her a solemn thumbs-up. It is easy to forget that a plan made in advance can carry you through a day when your mood will not.

On Thursday the rain was heavy and steady, but there was no thunder and no lightning, and she decided, after checking the sky, that it was safe to go out. She zipped up her yellow jacket and ran slowly along the empty street with a grim little smile, the water drumming on her hood and running in cold lines down her neck. Every sensible instinct told her to turn back, and she ran on, slowly and stubbornly.

Halfway round the park she stepped in a puddle so deep that the water poured over the top of her shoe, and at the same moment her hood blew back. She might have been furious, but instead she began to laugh, soaked to the skin and dripping like a fountain, and she discovered with some astonishment that she rather loved the rain. Discomfort, she was beginning to see, is so often the doorway to delight, and rain is only water after all.

The next morning she woke with a scratchy throat and a streaming nose, and she knew at once that the sensible thing was to stay indoors. She made tea, wrapped herself in a blanket and reminded herself that listening to the body is a part of training and never a betrayal of it. A stubborn kind of strength pushes on regardless, but a wise kind of strength knows when to stop.

In the final week the plan asked her to run a great deal less, so that her legs would be fresh and rested on the day of the race. It felt thoroughly wrong to do so little when the great test was so close, and her nervous mind kept whispering that she was not ready, but Hugo told her that the real work was already done. All she needed now, he said, was to trust the months of effort that she had already put into her legs.

Two days before the race Hugo cooked an enormous pot of pasta, and they ate it at his kitchen table with Pepper snoring gently beneath the chair. He told her about the time he had run a charity race in his full firefighter uniform, helmet and boots included. He had finished so red and so hot that he could hardly speak and had to be handed a bucket of water, but he still did not regret a single step.

On Saturday evening Dara laid out her kit on the bedroom chair in a neat row, with the running top, the number, the socks, the shoes and the water bottle all lined up like soldiers. She checked the list three times, and then a fourth time for good measure, and with every check she felt her nerves climbing a little higher. The thing she had wanted to prove to herself was now, quite literally, a matter of tomorrow morning.

She could not sleep, so she took her notebook, switched on the small lamp and wrote two words on a clean page: excited and scared. She allowed both of them to be true at once, and she remembered that a feeling that has been named loses some of its power to take her by surprise. After a little while she put down the pen, breathed out for a count of six and closed her eyes.

At five o'clock the alarm rang in the dark, and Dara dressed in silence, drank a glass of water and ate a banana standing at the kitchen window. When she opened the front door she found Hugo already waiting at her gate in his old green coat, with Pepper at his side, ready to walk with her to the bus stop. The street was silent, the sky was just beginning to pale, and the day she had been preparing for had finally arrived.

On race day the square in front of the Town Hall was packed with runners, and Dara stood among them in the cool grey light of dawn with her number pinned to her chest. Her stomach fluttered, her hands were cold and she could not decide whether she felt excited or terrified, which was probably the point. Music thumped from a loudspeaker, and a man with a microphone told everyone to enjoy themselves.

She looked around and saw people of every age, shape and speed, some of them in fancy dress and some in the green T-shirts of the food bank, and nobody at all was looking at her. It occurred to her that every one of them had once been a beginner in a pair of stiff new shoes, standing at the edge of something that seemed too big. The thought made her feel part of a very large and surprisingly friendly family.

Hugo walked her to the barrier with Pepper trotting beside him and offered the last piece of advice that he had been saving, in a low voice, as though it were a secret. Start slowly, he said, because the first kilometre is where everyone makes the same mistake, and run your own race, because all the others are running theirs. Then he held her by both shoulders for a moment, nodded and stepped back into the crowd.

A voice counted down from ten, the whole crowd leaned forward like a field of grass in the wind, and a horn sounded over a thousand heads. Dara drew a deep breath and began slowly on purpose, shuffling forward at the pace of the people around her until the pack at last began to thin. It was not a dramatic start, but it was exactly the start that she had planned.

In the first kilometre the excitement carried her along like a river, and she glanced at her watch and realised that she was running far faster than the plan. She remembered what she had promised herself, eased back to a gentle pace and let a group of cheerful runners surge on ahead without her. It was surprisingly hard to be passed so early, and surprisingly easy, once the feeling had faded, to be wise.

By the third kilometre she had found a steady rhythm, with the river glittering on her left and the road smooth and wet beneath her feet. People were clapping from the bridge, a man was playing a trumpet, and a small boy held out his hand to give her a high five as she passed. She slapped it, laughing, and felt strangely lifted by the kindness of people who did not even know her name.

At the five-kilometre mark she heard her name called, and there on the pavement were Leila, Samir and Nadia, holding the banner high above their heads, the purple dragon in the corner flapping wildly. Dara waved, laughed and cried all at the same time, and the sound of their shouting carried her forward for a long way afterwards. She had never before been cheered for something that she had chosen so deliberately.

At six kilometres her legs turned heavy, as if someone had filled her socks with sand, and a small twinge made itself known in her ankle. She slowed down at once and asked herself the question that Hugo had taught her, which was whether this was pain or only effort. After a moment's careful listening she decided that it was effort, the ordinary, honest kind, and she carried on.

At seven kilometres her mind began to make an extremely reasonable case for stopping, and every part of her wanted to quit. She did not argue with it; she simply walked at the edge of the road while runner after runner passed her by, and she felt the old shame rise in her throat. It was a feeling she knew well, and she noticed, to her surprise, that she could carry it and keep moving.

She drank some water, breathed out slowly for a count of six and chose a lamp post a short distance ahead as her next goal. She ran to it, and when she reached it she picked another, and then another, until the whole long road had been divided into pieces small enough to manage. A distance that seems impossible whole is always possible one lamp post at a time.

At eight kilometres she was dragging her feet, and her own breathing sounded loud and ragged in her ears, as if the whole world had been reduced to a single wheeze. Then a bright cap appeared at her shoulder, and Ines, who had been running her own slow race a little way behind, fell into step beside her and said cheerfully that they were nearly there. They would go on together, she announced, and no argument was possible, so Dara simply nodded and kept putting one foot in front of the other.

At nine kilometres the road curved into the gates of Linden Park, and both sides of the path were lined with spectators, clapping, ringing cowbells and waving flags and handwritten signs. Some read her name from the number on her chest and shouted it, and she smiled at every single one of them, since they could not possibly have known how much it meant. A stranger's cheer, she discovered, can lift the heart as surely as a hand beneath the elbow.

In the last kilometre she found herself thinking about the day she had carried a cardboard box onto a bus and then sat in a silent flat beside a cup of cold tea, convinced that her life had ended. The woman who had done that could not have imagined this morning, with its noise and its sunshine and its stubborn, aching legs, and the thought gave her a final reserve of strength. Everything that had happened since had been built, one small hard thing at a time, on the day that she had thought was the end.

At the end of the long path she saw the finishing arch shining in the sunshine, with a dense crowd roaring on either side of it. She lifted her knees, drew in a great ragged breath and ran towards it as fast as her tired body would carry her, and Ines, laughing, fell back and let her go ahead. Every muscle in her body complained loudly about the sudden change of plan, and she did not care in the least.

Dara crossed the finishing line with both arms raised high above her head, and laughter and tears came pouring out of her at the same time, so that she could not tell which was which. Her time was about an hour and twenty minutes, which was not fast by anyone's standards, but she had done it, every step of it, with her own two legs. In that bright, noisy, unrepeatable moment she did not want to be anywhere else on earth, or to be anyone else.

A volunteer in a bright orange jacket hung a medal around her neck and wrapped a rustling silver blanket around her shoulders, and Dara thanked her in a voice that did not sound like her own. She took a few unsteady steps before her legs announced firmly that they had given everything they had and would take no further instructions. She looked about her for somewhere, anywhere at all, to sit down before the whole world began gently to tilt.

She lowered herself onto the kerb in the warm sun, the medal heavy on her chest and the blanket crackling at her ears, and let the whole year pass slowly through her mind. The race had shown her that she was stronger than she had ever believed, though she understood that strength does not mean never hurting, and that she had been hurt many times along the way. It meant, rather, that she had gone on anyway, carrying the hurt with her, one small step after another.

Hugo found her first, with Pepper straining at the lead, and then Leila arrived at a half run with Samir and Nadia sprinting ahead of her and the banner trailing from one small fist. Everybody hugged her at once, and Hugo's eyes were suspiciously bright, and Nadia asked in a very serious voice whether she could please hold the medal. Dara lifted the ribbon over her head and hung the whole shining weight of it round her niece's neck.

They walked slowly to a small café near the park, where they ate an enormous breakfast of pancakes, bacon and strong tea at a table by the window. The medal travelled from hand to hand around the table, each person weighing it solemnly and pronouncing it very heavy, and nobody could stop talking at once. It was the loudest, happiest and most chaotic meal that Dara could remember, and she did not want it to end.

That night, after a long hot bath and a very short nap, Dara stood in front of the fridge in her dressing gown and added a new line to the list in the same blue pen. It said, I finished the Riverside Ten, and she hung the medal from the fridge handle beside it, where it swung gently and caught the light. She stood there for a long time in the quiet kitchen, quite unable to stop smiling at a medal and a sheet of paper.

A few days after the race Dara sat at the kitchen table with her medal beside her, and an odd, flat grey feeling settled over her like dust on a shelf. She could not explain it, because she had just done the hardest thing of her year and everyone she knew had told her how proud they were. Yet the sparkle had gone out of the morning, and the flat seemed very quiet.

On the park bench she told Hugo that she was afraid the old emptiness was returning, and that perhaps everything she had built was starting to crumble. He shook his head slowly and said that it is common to feel low after a big goal, because the long climb is over and the mind has not yet found its next mountain. It was no sign of failure, he told her, and it would pass in its own time.

Dara resolved to use her tools one at a time, as a carpenter reaches for each chisel in turn. She breathed in for four counts and out for six, wrote the word flat on a clean page and went for a short walk beside the river, watching the water slide towards the sea. By the end of the afternoon the feeling had not vanished, but it had lost its power to alarm her.

On Friday Ms Barrow asked her to stay behind, closed the door and explained that the company would very much like her to take a permanent position in the customer team. The pay was fair, the work was more interesting than she had expected and the people were kind, and Dara said yes with a smile that she did not try to hide. She walked out of the office feeling that the bridge Hugo had talked about had reached the far bank.

One evening Dara found a leaflet about a part-time course in managing projects, which met on Tuesday evenings at the city college. She had not sat in a classroom since she was nineteen, and the thought of it made her palms damp, so she filled in the form at once, before the clever part of her mind could invent an excuse. A new small hard thing, she thought, was exactly what the flat grey feeling had been waiting for.

A month later Dara slept through her alarm after a miserable night, missed her morning run and snapped at Kofi over some trivial mistake with a spreadsheet. By lunchtime she was crushed with shame, and the old voice, which had been quiet for weeks, murmured that she had not really changed at all. It was a plausible and poisonous suggestion, and she could feel herself beginning to believe it.

She stopped, breathed out slowly and reminded herself of the oldest lesson in her notebook, that one bad day is not a bad life. Then she went to the kitchen, made Kofi a coffee, told him honestly that she was sorry and discovered that he had forgotten the whole incident by ten past nine. Not every mistake, she saw, needs a funeral; some only need an apology and a fresh start.

On Sunday evenings Dara began a short review, with a mug of tea, a lamp and her notebook, and she asked herself three questions: what went well, what was hard and what one small thing would she do next week. It took no more than ten minutes, but it kept her habits from slipping away unnoticed, in the way that a quiet gardener keeps the weeds from taking over. She thought of it as a small, regular appointment with her own life, and she never once cancelled it.

One Sunday Leila rang, her voice thin with tiredness, to say that work and the children had worn her out entirely, and Dara went straight round on the bus. She made the tea, sat beside her on the sofa and listened without trying to repair anything, and she thought of all the times that her sister had done exactly this for her. It felt good to be the one with the strength to spare, and she realised that this, too, was part of the change.

In the autumn Hugo announced, in the casual tone of a man mentioning a parcel, that he needed an operation on his knee and would be resting for several weeks. Dara told him at once that she would walk Pepper every morning, and as she knocked on his door at seven the next day she noticed that, for once, she was the one doing the knocking. The old dog was in no hurry at all, and neither, as it turned out, was she, for the first time in years.

One evening in September Dara came home from work and found a young man sitting on the stairs with his head in his hands and a rucksack at his feet. He was Ben, nineteen years old, the new tenant of flat three, and he looked like someone who had not slept properly for days. She almost walked past, and then she remembered how it felt to be passed.

She did not tell him to cheer up or bombard him with questions; instead she sat down two steps below him, put her shopping on the floor and waited in the dim light of the landing. After a while he said quietly that it had been a rough month, and she answered that she had time to listen. Sometimes the kindest thing to offer a person is not a solution but an unhurried silence.

Ben told her, haltingly, that he had abandoned his college course halfway through the first year and that his parents did not yet know. He felt like a complete failure, he said, and she recognised the emptiness in his voice at once, since she had once carried it out of an office in a cardboard box. It is a strange comfort to discover that another person has stood in the same cold place.

She told him that feelings cannot be hurried and that one bad chapter does not make a bad book, and she took care not to say it as if it were a speech. Then she offered him a mug of tea and invited him to join her and an elderly spaniel for a walk the next morning, and he said, with a shrug, that he might. It was neither a promise nor a refusal, and she left it at that.

To her surprise Ben knocked on her door at seven the next day, and the three of them wandered slowly through Linden Park while Pepper investigated every tree. When Dara mentioned her rule of one small hard thing each day, he took out his phone with a sigh and typed a short, awkward email to his tutor asking for a meeting. It was a tiny act, but she watched his shoulders ease a little as he pressed send.

A few weeks later Dara noticed that Ben looked worse, thinner and greyer, and that his plate always seemed to be full when she saw it through his open door. He told her in a flat, tired voice that there was no point in any of it, and the words made her stomach tighten, because they sounded different from ordinary sadness. She understood, with a small cold shock, that this was a moment when listening alone was no longer enough.

She sat across from him in his small, untidy flat and asked, as gently and calmly as she could manage, whether he ever had thoughts of ending his life. She had read that asking directly does not make things worse and often brings relief, and she held his gaze steadily while she waited. After a long silence Ben nodded and said, in a voice barely above a whisper, that sometimes he did.

Dara did not panic, and she did not argue; she told him that she was glad he had said it aloud and that he deserved help from someone trained to give it. She sat beside him while he telephoned his doctor's surgery and made an appointment for the next morning, and she saved the number of a crisis line in her own phone in case it was needed. If anyone is ever in immediate danger, she knew, the right call is to the emergency services.

Hugo, who was walking again with a stick, joined them on a bench in the sunshine and told them both about a terrible rescue many years before that had left him unable to sleep for months. A counsellor had helped him find his feet again, he said, and asking for that help had been the wisest decision of his whole life, far wiser than any he had made on a fire engine. Ben listened with his eyes fixed on the grass and did not say a word.

That evening Dara sat with Leila in the bright quiet of her sister's living room and admitted that she had experienced heavy nights of her own during that long year, nights when the dark had seemed to have no ending. Leila took her hand and said nothing for a while, and then Dara decided to book a counsellor. It was not because she was in danger but because she wanted a skilled person to help her carry what she was carrying, and strength, she thought, includes knowing when to ask.

In her first session Ms Hale listened with complete attention, asked a few quiet questions and never once told Dara what she ought to feel. Dara came to understand that counselling is simply a skilled kind of conversation with a person trained to help you sort the tangle, and that it is meant for ordinary people with ordinary heavy days. She walked out into the evening feeling that she had put down a bag she had been carrying without noticing.

A month later Ben had started a different course at a different college, and he had a weekly appointment with a doctor who took him seriously. He still had hard days, and Dara still sat with him on the stairs now and then, but he had people around him and a plan to turn to when the dark came, and that made all the difference. Recovery, she was learning, is rarely a straight line and almost never a solitary one.

In March, a year to the week after she had walked out of Marlow Shoes, Dara opened the hall cupboard and found the old cardboard box on the top shelf. She stood looking at the dusty, slightly crushed thing for a long moment and then smiled, as though it were an old friend who had been with her through the very worst of it. It had once held everything she thought she had left, and it seemed so much smaller now.

She decided that the box deserved a new purpose, and she filled it with her notebooks, the list that had hung on the fridge and the medal on its faded ribbon. It no longer held what she had lost, but rather the proof of everything she had done since, and she closed the lid with a feeling of quiet satisfaction. Some day, she thought, she might show it to a child, or a stranger on a staircase, as evidence that a bad chapter can be survived.

On a still evening Dara walked along Alder Road with Hugo and Pepper, and Hugo, whose knee was much improved, asked her what had really changed that year. She took a long time to answer, and when she did she said that she still hurt sometimes and still doubted herself, but that she no longer faced it alone. She no longer believed every story her mind told her, either, and that, said Hugo, was precisely what he had meant by strong.

On Sunday she cooked an enormous dinner in her small flat for Leila, the children, Hugo, Mina, Ben and Ines, and they all squeezed around a long table made of two smaller ones pushed together. Dara thanked every person there in turn, rather clumsily, and the room filled up with so much noise and laughter that the neighbours downstairs banged on the ceiling, in a friendly way. She had never in her whole life felt so wonderfully crowded, or so deeply and quietly content.

Early the following Saturday Dara climbed the long hill in Linden Park with Pepper plodding at her side, before a single other soul was awake, and she did not need to be asked to go. At the top she stopped to catch her breath and looked out over the grey roofs, the glint of the river and the Town Hall tower, as the first light came creeping across the city. The view had been there all along, waiting for her to climb to it.

She sat down on the bench at the summit, took out her notebook and began to write what she had learned, in plain words, without any fancy phrases. She was writing it for herself, because memory is a poor keeper of lessons, and she was also writing it for Ben, in the hope that someday he would find it useful. Her pen moved steadily, and the page began to fill with the small bright facts of a hard year.

Her lessons were short and simple: feel what you feel, speak to yourself with kindness, breathe out slowly, take the next small step, ask for help and look after your body. She added that rest is a part of the plan and not a break from it, and that nobody has ever had to climb alone, however long it may feel as if they do. She read the list through once, and then she put the pen down and watched the sun lift above the roofs.

The truth that Dara carried out of that difficult year was a simple one: you are very likely stronger than you think, and your strength grows each time you use it. Allow yourself to feel what you feel, speak to yourself kindly, take the next small step, ask for help and look after your body, and then step a little outside your comfort zone again tomorrow. You do not have to feel brave to begin; you only have to begin.
